question: The vast majority of dogs in the world are not pets — they are working animals or semi-wild village dogs that earn their food. About 75-85% of the world's roughly 900 million dogs fall in that group. What does that tell us about the domestication story?
choices: Dogs evolved alongside humans as working partners — the pet relationship is a recent minority
Dogs were always meant to be pets — the working dogs are descendants of escaped house dogs
Dogs are split into two species — the working dogs and the pet dogs are now genetically separate
Dogs in the wild started as pets that ran away — every village dog is a returned house dog
answer: Dogs evolved alongside humans as working partners — the pet relationship is a recent minority
context: Coppinger and Coppinger (Dogs: A Startling New Understanding, 2001) and global census estimates put working / village dogs at 75-85% of the dog population. The companion-animal pet is a Western late-modern relationship; the dog-as-partner story is older and broader.

question: The first major US federal wildlife law was passed in 1900, championed by Iowa congressman John Lacey. It made it a federal crime to transport across state lines any wildlife taken in violation of another state's laws. Why did the Lacey Act matter so much?
choices: Market hunters could no longer skirt state bag limits by selling kills across state lines
It banned all hunting on federal land for the first time in American legal history
It set up the national park system that Theodore Roosevelt expanded under his presidency
It paid hunters directly from federal taxes whenever they reported a poacher to authorities
answer: Market hunters could no longer skirt state bag limits by selling kills across state lines
context: The Lacey Act (1900) was a market-hunting kill switch. Until then, market hunters slaughtered passenger pigeons, bison, waterfowl, and shipped the meat anywhere it sold. Federal jurisdiction over interstate wildlife traffic was the spine state laws had needed.

question: In 1887 Theodore Roosevelt and George Bird Grinnell founded a club whose members had to have taken three different North American big-game species by fair-chase methods. Why was the club organized this way?
choices: Working hunters could best lobby for the wildlife protections needed to keep their sport alive
Big-game hunters could compete to set records and prove their skill on the largest animals
Wealthy hunters could pool funds to import African big game into private American preserves
Hunters could compare gun and ammunition makers to advance the technology of firearms
answer: Working hunters could best lobby for the wildlife protections needed to keep their sport alive
context: The Boone and Crockett Club (1887) is the oldest American conservation organization. Roosevelt's premise: hunters, who knew wildlife, had to be the political muscle behind protection. The club drove the Lacey Act, the Yellowstone protections, and the early national-forest system.

question: The Migratory Bird Treaty Act of 1918 was the United States' first major federal step into protecting non-game birds. What concrete problem was it built to stop?
choices: Plume hunting — feathers from egrets, herons, and other birds harvested for women's hats
Pesticide spraying — early DDT campaigns wiping out songbirds in eastern farm states
Habitat loss — vast wetland drainage in the Midwest reducing breeding grounds for ducks
Lead poisoning — spent shot in marshlands killing waterfowl that ingested the pellets
answer: Plume hunting — feathers from egrets, herons, and other birds harvested for women's hats
context: Late 1800s women's hats demanded feathers — and millions of egrets, herons, and terns were slaughtered. The Audubon movement built around stopping it; the MBTA (with Canada, 1916) closed the trade. Working law for working wildlife.

question: Pittman-Robertson (1937) takes an 11% federal excise tax on firearms and ammunition and routes it to state wildlife restoration. Who effectively funds the program?
choices: Hunters and recreational shooters — people who buy firearms and ammunition fund the program directly
The general taxpayer — federal income tax fills the program's main accounts through the general fund
Manufacturers alone — gun and ammunition companies absorb the tax as a corporate fee on their own
International donors — World Wildlife Fund and other partners fill the gap each year through grants
answer: Hunters and recreational shooters — people who buy firearms and ammunition fund the program directly
context: Pittman-Robertson is the user-pays model: hunters fund the restoration of the wildlife they hunt. Since 1937 it has generated billions of dollars for state agencies. Dingell-Johnson (1950) does the same for anglers and fishing tackle. The North American Model's funding spine.

question: In 1900 fewer than 30,000 wild turkeys remained in the United States — habitat loss and market hunting had nearly finished the species. By 2010 the population was over 6 million. What recovery method drove the change?
choices: Trap-and-transfer — state wildlife agencies caught wild birds and released them in vacant habitat across all 49 states
Pen breeding — turkeys raised on farms were released into the wild and allowed to spread on their own
Habitat protection alone — forests were left untouched and turkeys found their own way back across the country
Predator removal — coyotes, foxes, and raptors were trapped out of turkey country across the south
answer: Trap-and-transfer — state wildlife agencies caught wild birds and released them in vacant habitat across all 49 states
context: Hand-rearing failed — pen-raised turkeys could not survive. Rocket-net trapping of wild birds and translocation, funded by Pittman-Robertson and the National Wild Turkey Federation (1973), drove the recovery. State agencies + hunters + working biology.

question: American whitetail deer numbered about 500,000 in 1900 — gone from much of their range. The population today is over 30 million. What combination drove the recovery?
choices: Regulated hunting seasons, habitat management, and refuge protection funded by hunter dollars
A complete hunting ban for fifty years until populations recovered to their original numbers
Captive breeding programs run by federal wildlife agencies on protected federal lands
International protection treaties that stopped commercial deer-product trade across borders
answer: Regulated hunting seasons, habitat management, and refuge protection funded by hunter dollars
context: The whitetail recovery is the most dramatic in American wildlife history. Regulated hunting (replacing market hunting), habitat work funded by hunter dollars, and refuges combined. Modern populations are sometimes too HIGH — managed hunting is the population control.

question: American bison numbered 30-60 million in 1800 and 1,000 by 1900. The recovery to over 500,000 today came through a coalition of private ranchers, tribal nations, the American Bison Society (1905), and federal agencies. What was the bison's role in plains ecosystems?
choices: A keystone grazer — bison wallows, grazing patterns, and dung created varied grassland habitat for many other species
An apex predator — bison hunting of prairie dogs and small mammals kept rodent populations in check
A migratory traveler — bison movements carried seeds and nutrients between regions of the plains
A timber clearer — bison stripped bark from trees, holding back forest encroachment on the prairies
answer: A keystone grazer — bison wallows, grazing patterns, and dung created varied grassland habitat for many other species
context: Bison wallows depress earth into shallow pools used by many species; their grazing creates a mosaic; their hooves break up sod. The American Bison Society was founded in 1905 by William Hornaday and Roosevelt. The recovery is a Western-stewardship case study.

question: American beavers were trapped to near-extinction by 1900 — the fur trade had run for two centuries. Modern populations are over 10 million. Why does beaver recovery matter for whole watersheds, not just the species?
choices: Beaver dams create wetlands that filter water, store snowmelt, and recharge groundwater across landscapes
Beaver fur farms produce premium pelts that fund state wildlife agencies more than other species
Beaver populations control river otter numbers by competing with otters for prime den sites
Beavers cut down spruce and pine trees that crowd out the maples favored by fall tourism
answer: Beaver dams create wetlands that filter water, store snowmelt, and recharge groundwater across landscapes
context: The beaver is a working ecosystem engineer. Restored beaver populations have brought back wet meadows, filtered watersheds, recharged groundwater, and helped fish populations across the American West. Conservation done by use plus regulation.

question: Aldo Leopold tells in 'Thinking Like a Mountain' (Sand County Almanac, 1949) how he shot a wolf as a young Forest Service officer and watched a 'fierce green fire' die in its eyes. What did the mountain teach him over the decades?
choices: Removing the wolf left deer to overbrowse — the system was not improved by killing the predator
Removing the wolf raised deer for hunters — the mountain prospered without large predators
Removing the wolf had no measurable effect — the mountain absorbed the loss easily
Removing the wolf brought elk in to replace it — one predator simply followed another
answer: Removing the wolf left deer to overbrowse — the system was not improved by killing the predator
context: Leopold's predator-control regret is the founding story of American ecological thought. The deer multiplied; the browse line crept up the mountain; the slopes washed bare. He learned to see the predator's place in the system — a key step toward the land ethic.

question: The Endangered Species Act of 1973 listed the bald eagle, peregrine falcon, and brown pelican among others. By the 2000s, all three were delisted as recovered. What was the dominant cause of their decline that the ESA helped to address?
choices: DDT pesticide use, which thinned eggshells in raptors and fish-eating birds across the country
Sport-hunting pressure on the species during the early decades of the twentieth century
Habitat loss from agricultural drainage of major wetlands during the post-war years
Lead poisoning from spent fishing tackle and shotgun pellets in their freshwater food sources
answer: DDT pesticide use, which thinned eggshells in raptors and fish-eating birds across the country
context: DDT (banned in 1972 in the US after Rachel Carson's Silent Spring, 1962) thinned shells of raptors and fish-eaters. ESA protection plus DDT ban allowed recovery. Bald eagle delisted 2007, peregrine 1999, brown pelican 2009 — major ESA success stories.

question: John Muir founded the Sierra Club and pushed for national parks where wilderness would be set aside from any commercial use. Gifford Pinchot founded the US Forest Service and argued for 'wise use' — sustainable timber, grazing, water for the many. What kind of disagreement was this?
choices: Preservation versus conservation — set-aside untouched versus regulated sustainable use
Public versus private — federal ownership versus state and private landowner control
Eastern versus Western — Atlantic conservation traditions versus Pacific-coast traditions
Religious versus secular — Muir's spiritual reverence versus Pinchot's secular utilitarianism
answer: Preservation versus conservation — set-aside untouched versus regulated sustainable use
context: Muir and Pinchot were both Roosevelt allies but split on Hetch Hetchy (the 1913 dam debate). Both traditions are American conservation. Pinchot's 'wise use' framework is the operating model of national forests; Muir's set-aside framework runs the national parks. Both legitimate; both real.

question: African elephant populations crashed under unregulated poaching for ivory in the late twentieth century. In southern Africa, several countries adopted a sustainable-use model: regulated hunting, community ownership of wildlife rights, ivory stockpile management. What happened to elephant numbers in those countries?
choices: Populations grew — community ownership gave locals economic reason to protect elephants
Populations crashed — regulated hunting accelerated the decline already underway
Populations stayed flat — sustainable use produced no measurable improvement either way
Populations were artificially boosted — captured zoo-bred elephants supplemented wild herds
answer: Populations grew — community ownership gave locals economic reason to protect elephants
context: Botswana, Namibia, Zimbabwe, and South Africa adopted community-conservancy and sustainable-use models in the 1980s-90s. Elephant numbers rose in those countries while crashing in unregulated regions. Conservation by use — controversial, but the data is real.

question: About 15 million Americans hunt each year and another 50 million fish. Through licenses, tags, equipment excise taxes, and direct contributions, they provide most of the funding for state wildlife agencies. What is the structural implication?
choices: Wildlife restoration is funded by the users of wildlife — incentives align with sustaining the resource itself
Wildlife funding rises and falls with hunter and angler numbers — declining participation strains the agencies
Wildlife funding comes from non-hunters — a political minority subsidizes the agencies for everyone else
Wildlife management is privatized — state agencies are effectively private clubs run by hunters and anglers
answer: Wildlife restoration is funded by the users of wildlife — incentives align with sustaining the resource itself
context: In most states, hunter and angler dollars cover 60-80% of fish-and-wildlife agency budgets. The structural lesson: the user-pays model ties recovery to sustained use. Declining hunter numbers (a real trend) is the funding-side challenge of the next decades.

question: The North American Model of Wildlife Conservation rests on seven principles, including 'wildlife is held in the public trust' (the public owns wildlife) and 'commerce in wildlife is regulated.' Which other principle is core to the model?
choices: Hunting opportunity is available to every citizen — democracy of the harvest, not a privilege of the elite
Hunting is reserved for citizens with property — only landowners may legally hunt on most lands
Hunting is restricted to a small federal license pool — the federal government caps total hunter numbers
Hunting is forbidden on all public land — wildlife on federal lands is left strictly untouched
answer: Hunting opportunity is available to every citizen — democracy of the harvest, not a privilege of the elite
context: Seven sisters of the North American Model: public trust, eliminate market hunting, allocation by law, hunting for legitimate purposes, wildlife as international resource, science-based management, democracy of hunting. The democratic-access principle distinguishes North American conservation from European aristocratic-hunting traditions.

question: Theodore Roosevelt during his presidency (1901-1909) set aside about 230 million acres of public land — national parks, national forests, national monuments, national wildlife refuges. Which of these designations did Roosevelt establish as a new category?
choices: National wildlife refuges — Pelican Island, Florida (1903) was the first ever in the US
National parks — Yellowstone had been a park since 1872, before Roosevelt was president
National forests — created by the Forest Reserve Act of 1891, before Roosevelt's term began
National monuments — established by Congress only after Roosevelt left the presidency in 1909
answer: National wildlife refuges — Pelican Island, Florida (1903) was the first ever in the US
context: Roosevelt founded the National Wildlife Refuge system in 1903 at Pelican Island. He also signed the Antiquities Act (1906), expanded the national forests massively, and championed the still-young National Park concept. The substantive American conservation founder.

question: Standard textbooks teach that humans domesticated dogs by capturing and taming wolf cubs. Genetic and behavioral evidence increasingly points to a different story. What is the leading alternative?
choices: Wolves with low fear of humans scavenged human camps and self-selected for tameness, starting the partnership
Wolves were captured from forests across Eurasia and bred in pens by Stone Age humans simultaneously
Modern dogs descend from a wholly separate canid never connected to wolves before domestication began
Wolves were domesticated only once in northern Europe and spread by ancient human migration outward
answer: Wolves with low fear of humans scavenged human camps and self-selected for tameness, starting the partnership
context: Coppinger's commensal-pathway hypothesis: wolves with tamer behavior survived better near human refuse; humans tolerated and eventually allied with them. The dogs that arose were partners, not captured pets. Some authors argue dogs domesticated themselves more than humans domesticated them.

question: A scholar argues: 'Animal welfare matters and we should breed, raise, and harvest livestock with attention to humane practice. But animals do not have rights identical to persons. The pasturing farmer and the regulated hunter are good stewards, not moral failures.' Which tradition does this argue from?
choices: Stewardship — humans are inside the biotic community with duties of humane husbandry but not animal-personhood
Singer-style impartialism — equal consideration of interests across species, with no presumption favoring human use
Cartesian instrumentalism — animals lack moral standing entirely, freeing humans to use them by any means
Animal rights legalism — non-human animals carry legal personhood with full standing in courts
answer: Stewardship — humans are inside the biotic community with duties of humane husbandry but not animal-personhood
context: Stewardship runs from Aquinas through Roosevelt and Leopold to the North American Model. Humane treatment YES; rights-as-personhood NO. The bank teaches this as the substantive Western position; Singer-style impartialism, Cartesian instrumentalism, and animal-rights legalism appear as positions to scrutinize against it.

question: A forester writes: 'A forest left untouched is not a forest preserved — it is a forest waiting to burn. Sustainable harvest, grazing rotations, and careful fire management are the working stewardship of American public land. Lock-it-away preservation is an aesthetic, not a strategy.' Which tradition is the forester defending?
choices: Pinchot-style conservation — wise use, sustained yield, multi-use management of public land
Muir-style preservationism — set-aside wilderness with minimal human management permitted
Singer-style impartialism — wildlife has standing equal to human interests in any decision
Cartesian instrumentalism — public land exists for whatever human use produces the most value
answer: Pinchot-style conservation — wise use, sustained yield, multi-use management of public land
context: Gifford Pinchot founded the US Forest Service in 1905 on the doctrine of 'wise use' — sustainable timber, grazing, water for the many. John Muir's preservationism (Sierra Club, national parks) treats wilderness as an end in itself. Both legitimate; this scholar is in Pinchot's tradition. The Hetch Hetchy debate (1913) crystallized the split.

question: An animal-rights philosopher argues: 'Species membership is not a morally relevant trait. Pain felt by a pig and pain felt by a person count equally in any ethical calculation, regardless of whether the pig is being raised for food.' What is the critic's structural response?
choices: Partiality — the same logic would forbid parents from prioritizing their own children over strangers and erodes most moral practice
Hedonism — the argument reduces all ethics to a single dimension and ignores rights as a distinct category of moral concern
Scientism — the argument depends on pain measurement we cannot actually perform across very different species
Sentimentalism — the argument trades on emotion rather than reason and is therefore not philosophically serious
answer: Partiality — the same logic would forbid parents from prioritizing their own children over strangers and erodes most moral practice
context: Singer's impartialism (Animal Liberation, 1975) is best critiqued on the partiality structure: it would also forbid parents from preferring their own children, citizens preferring their countrymen, etc. The same abstract demand collapses most actual moral practice. The bank teaches the move, not a verdict.

question: Section 7 of the Endangered Species Act requires federal agencies to consult before undertaking any action that 'may affect' a listed species. Defenders cite recovery of the bald eagle and peregrine falcon. Critics raise a specific structural concern. What is it?
choices: Section 7 can block infrastructure indefinitely on consultation grounds, with little proportionality across actions
Section 7 funds federal agencies directly and creates an incentive to over-list species for budgetary reasons
Section 7 transfers wildlife jurisdiction to states and weakens uniform federal protection nationwide
Section 7 was struck down in 1995 and is no longer the operative consultation rule under federal law
answer: Section 7 can block infrastructure indefinitely on consultation grounds, with little proportionality across actions
context: Section 7 consultation (Tennessee Valley Authority v. Hill, 1978 — the snail darter case) can halt federal projects. Recovery wins are real (bald eagle, peregrine, brown pelican delisted). Critique: the standard is 'may affect,' which leaves wide discretion. The bank teaches structural critique without verdict.

question: Theodore Roosevelt's writings on the West ('Hunting Trips of a Ranchman' 1885, 'Ranch Life and the Hunting-Trail' 1888) frame hunting as a school of character — endurance, observation, moral seriousness about the animal taken. This is what Leopold later called what?
choices: The 'split-rail value' of wildlife — moral and cultural goods produced by the experience of hunting and being in nature
The 'public trust doctrine' — the legal mechanism by which wildlife is owned by the people of each state
The 'fair chase' standard — the technical rules by which the Boone and Crockett Club records game animals
The 'preservationist creed' — the ethical principle that wildlife should be left untouched by humans entirely
answer: The 'split-rail value' of wildlife — moral and cultural goods produced by the experience of hunting and being in nature
context: Leopold's Sand County Almanac uses 'split-rail value' for the moral, cultural, and character goods of being out in wildlife country — the things hunting and woodscraft produce in a person beyond meat or trophy. Roosevelt is the substantive writer in this tradition; Leopold named it.

question: Aquinas (Summa Theologiae IIa-IIae) holds that humans hold rational dominion over animals in the divine order of creation, but the dominion is governance and stewardship, not exploitation. What follows from his medieval Christian account?
choices: Humans may use animals for food, work, and material, but cruelty is forbidden because it corrupts the soul of the user
Humans may not use animals for any purpose at all because animals share rational souls equally with human persons
Humans may use animals freely without any restriction whatever because animals lack souls of any kind whatsoever
Humans must offer formal ritual sacrifice for any animal taken in food production or in working partnership at all
answer: Humans may use animals for food, work, and material, but cruelty is forbidden because it corrupts the soul of the user
context: Aquinas: dominion includes use but forbids cruelty. The reason is structural — gratuitous cruelty corrupts the user and disorders the will. Stewardship, not exploitation; husbandry, not personhood. The intellectual root of Western humane-treatment tradition that runs through Roosevelt and Leopold.

question: Aristotle (History of Animals, Politics I) ordered living things on a 'scala naturae' — a graded ranking from simplest plants up through animals to humans. Modern biology has largely set this aside. But one philosophical commitment of Aristotle's framing survives in Western stewardship thought. Which?
choices: That humans have a distinctive moral standing — rational beings with duties of governance over the natural order
That all life is morally equivalent — the chain was only a description, not a ranking of moral importance
That nature has no moral standing at all — only humans participate in moral consideration of any sort
That plants share rationality with animals — both kinds of life have the same moral standing in his view
answer: That humans have a distinctive moral standing — rational beings with duties of governance over the natural order
context: Aristotle's ordering had hierarchy but also continuity. The Western stewardship tradition keeps the moral-governance idea (humans as rational beings with duties of care) while dropping the literal ladder. Aquinas built on Aristotle; Roosevelt and Leopold inherited the structure without the ladder. Modern biology, ancient ethic.

question: CITES (Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species, 1973) regulates the global wildlife trade. Some southern African nations argue CITES restrictions on ivory have hurt their conservation by removing market incentives for landowners to tolerate elephants. What kind of disagreement is this?
choices: Sustainable-use versus exclusion — whether conservation works through regulated trade or through near-total prohibition
Public versus private — whether national governments or local landowners should set wildlife policy
Hunter versus angler — whether terrestrial wildlife or fisheries should receive the larger share of funding
Domestic versus international — whether national or treaty-based rules should govern wildlife law
answer: Sustainable-use versus exclusion — whether conservation works through regulated trade or through near-total prohibition
context: Botswana, Namibia, Zimbabwe, South Africa argue community ownership + regulated harvest produced their elephant recoveries; CITES bans removed those incentives. The disagreement is structural: does conservation work better through user-pays or set-aside? Same question Pinchot vs Muir asked, on a global scale.

question: Aldo Leopold's land ethic, in 'A Sand County Almanac' (1949), states: 'A thing is right when it tends to preserve the integrity, stability, and beauty of the biotic community.' What move does this make against pure preservationism?
choices: The land ethic includes humans as members of the biotic community, not extracted observers from it
The land ethic requires humans to leave the biotic community alone entirely so it can be preserved
The land ethic limits wildlife protection to species considered useful to humans for food or for sport
The land ethic assigns legal personhood to ecosystems, allowing rivers and forests to sue in court
answer: The land ethic includes humans as members of the biotic community, not extracted observers from it
context: Leopold's key move: humans are members of the biotic community. Use is part of belonging; reckless use is a betrayal of membership. This is not Muir's set-aside preservationism and not Singer's species-equal impartialism — it is stewardship with humans inside the system. The substantive American moral tradition on wildlife.

question: Modern military and police K-9 training relies on operant conditioning: paired target-scent and reward, refined through thousands of repetitions. What does the working-dog evidence suggest about the wolf-to-dog transition more broadly?
choices: Domestication selected for trainability — dogs find human-led learning rewarding in ways their wolf ancestors do not
Domestication selected for raw intelligence — dogs solve novel problems better than wolves on most measured tasks
Domestication selected for body size — dogs are physically smaller and easier for humans to handle than wolves
Domestication selected for diet — dogs digest human leftovers better than wolves digest the same food
answer: Domestication selected for trainability — dogs find human-led learning rewarding in ways their wolf ancestors do not
context: Hare and Tomasello's work on dog social cognition: dogs are not 'smarter' than wolves but are wired to find human-coordinated tasks rewarding. The training-payoff loop that produces modern K-9s rides on a domestication-selected substrate. Working dogs are the legible end of a deep partnership.

question: Peter Singer's animal-liberation argument runs: if pain matters morally, and a chicken can feel pain, then a chicken's pain matters morally — and species membership cannot be the basis of differential moral concern. Critics from the Western stewardship tradition reply structurally. What is the strongest reply?
choices: Moral relations rest on partiality and species kinship — a parent's child, a community's members, a species' kin all carry just preferences
Pain is not the only morally relevant fact — animals lack rational standing entirely and therefore cannot enter moral concern at all
Singer is empirically wrong about chicken pain — modern neuroscience shows chickens lack the brain structures for any pain
Singer is logically inconsistent — his argument also forbids using plants for food because plants respond to stimuli too
answer: Moral relations rest on partiality and species kinship — a parent's child, a community's members, a species' kin all carry just preferences
context: Partiality is the structural response: Singer's impartialism would forbid parents preferring their children, citizens preferring countrymen, neighbors preferring neighbors. Cottingham (Partiality and the Virtues, 1998), Williams ('one thought too many'). The stewardship tradition allows partiality AND humane treatment — not all-or-nothing.

question: Theodore Roosevelt was a serious Reformed Christian whose conservation writing draws explicitly on stewardship language — 'the heritage of our children,' 'we are not the owners but the trustees.' The framing fits which deeper tradition?
choices: Christian dominion-as-stewardship — humans entrusted with the created order, accountable for its sustained flourishing
Greek pantheism — every part of nature is divine and humans owe ritual reverence to specific natural features
Eastern non-attachment — humans should withdraw from the natural world to leave it undisturbed by use
Enlightenment naturalism — nature is a mechanism with no normative claim on humans of any sort
answer: Christian dominion-as-stewardship — humans entrusted with the created order, accountable for its sustained flourishing
context: Roosevelt drew on the Reformed Protestant 'trustee' framing of Genesis 1-2 — dominion as stewardship, not exploitation. The Aquinas-through-Reformed-tradition line is the deep Christian root of American conservation. Roosevelt is the political expression; the theological framing is older than him by centuries.

question: Leopold and Roosevelt both argue that hunting is morally formative — not despite the killing but in some sense because of it. The hunter sees the animal, the country, and the kill with seriousness. What is the structural claim?
choices: Direct contact with the harvest — including the killing — forces moral honesty that purchased food cannot teach
Hunting is a sport like any other sport — its only value is recreation and any moral framing is rationalization
Hunting is morally suspect but legally permitted — the formation claim is propaganda to justify a contested activity
Hunting produces material wealth — the formation is incidental and the activity is justified on economic grounds alone
answer: Direct contact with the harvest — including the killing — forces moral honesty that purchased food cannot teach
context: Roosevelt and Leopold's claim: meat in plastic at the grocery store severs the eater from the kill. Hunting puts the eater back in the relation — and the discipline that follows (fair chase, full use, knowing the country) is moral formation. The bank teaches the move, not a verdict. Real intellectual tradition.

question: Charles Darwin's 'The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals' (1872) argued that emotional displays share evolutionary continuity across species — a fear-bared tooth in a chimpanzee, a defensive snarl in a wolf, a flinch in a human. What broader thesis was Darwin defending?
choices: Continuity of mind — emotional and mental life are not unique to humans but graded across animal lineages
Equality of moral standing — animals are morally equivalent to humans because they share emotional repertoires
Speech precedes emotion — language is the source of human emotional life, absent in any animal
Emotion is purely cultural — facial displays vary so widely across cultures that no shared biology exists
answer: Continuity of mind — emotional and mental life are not unique to humans but graded across animal lineages
context: Darwin's continuity thesis: mind is not a uniquely human phenomenon but a graded one across animal life. He distinguished this from moral equivalence (which he did not argue). The thesis grounds modern animal cognition research from Frans de Waal to Marc Hauser. Continuity yes; species-equal moral standing — a separate question entirely.

question: Carrier pigeons used in military service across both world wars find their home loft from hundreds of miles away across unfamiliar country. Decades of research have identified at least three distinct cues the pigeons use in combination. Which is one of them?
choices: Magnetoreception — iron-mineral receptors in the beak detect the Earth's magnetic field as a compass cue
Echolocation — pigeons emit sonar clicks during flight and reconstruct the landscape from returning echoes
Stellar fix — pigeons recognize specific star patterns and orient by them during night flights home alone
Genetic memory — each pigeon carries an inherited map of its breed's ancestral home loft locations
answer: Magnetoreception — iron-mineral receptors in the beak detect the Earth's magnetic field as a compass cue
context: Pigeon navigation combines sun-compass, magnetoreception (iron in the beak), and olfactory cues from atmospheric trails. Mora et al. (Nature, 2004) localized the magnetic receptor; Wallraff (2005) reviewed the olfactory map. Working partners with us in war; biological wonders on their own.

question: Aldo Leopold's predator-control regret ('Thinking Like a Mountain') is sometimes read as a rejection of all use and management of wildlife. Leopold himself remained a lifelong deer hunter. Which reading of his position is most consistent with the full text?
choices: Stewardship as ecological literacy — humans manage the system best when they understand the place of predators and prey within it
Strict preservationism — all human use of wildlife is morally wrong once we understand ecosystem complexity
Animal-rights universalism — predators have rights equal to prey, so all hunting must be restricted equally
Pure utilitarianism — wildlife management should maximize aggregate animal welfare regardless of species identity
answer: Stewardship as ecological literacy — humans manage the system best when they understand the place of predators and prey within it
context: Leopold the wolf-killer who learned, hunted, and wrote on through the rest of his life. The lesson was not 'stop using' but 'see the system whole' — the predator's place in the cycle of deer and forest. Stewardship is ecological literacy plus humane practice plus continued use. The full Leopold.

question: When floodwaters rise over their nest, fire ants do something amazing — they link their bodies together to make a giant floating raft. What part of the ant keeps the raft from sinking?
answer: Tiny hairs on their bodies that trap a layer of air
choices: Tiny hairs on their bodies that trap a layer of air
Wax on their feet that pushes the water away
Empty gas bubbles inside their stomach pouches
Stiff wings stretched out flat over the surface
context: Fire ant rafts can float for weeks. Tiny body hairs trap air pockets, making the linked ants act like one giant waterproof patch.

question: Tiny ants march down a forest trail with bits of leaf held high over their heads — but the ants never eat those leaves. Why are they carrying them home?
answer: They feed the leaves to a fungus farm and eat the fungus
choices: They feed the leaves to a fungus farm and eat the fungus
They use the leaves to wrap and cool the queen's chamber
They lay the leaves to mark a trail back from new spots
They store the leaves as cold-weather food for the winter
context: Leafcutter ants run underground fungus farms older than human farming. The fungus digests cellulose the ants cannot. They eat only the fungus.

question: A honeybee finds a great patch of flowers. Back at the hive, she does a wiggly little dance. What is the dance telling the other bees?
answer: Where the flowers are, and how far away to fly
choices: Where the flowers are, and how far away to fly
How sweet the nectar tasted on her flight back
How many other bees should leave at one time
Which sister bee discovered the flowers first
context: A waggle dance encodes direction (angle vs vertical) and distance (waggle length). Karl von Frisch won a Nobel Prize for decoding it.

question: A small beetle has a wild defense — when a frog or ant tries to grab it, the beetle sprays scalding-hot liquid right at the attacker. How hot is the spray?
answer: Near 100 degrees Celsius — almost boiling water
choices: Near 100 degrees Celsius — almost boiling water
Near 40 degrees Celsius — warm like a bath
Near 60 degrees Celsius — like very hot tap water
Near 0 degrees Celsius — icy cold to numb the foe
context: The bombardier beetle's spray comes out near 100°C, hot enough to burn skin and stop almost any small attacker.

question: A jumping spider has only eight eyes — but some kinds can see more colors than you can. How do scientists know the spider sees these extra colors?
answer: Their eyes carry special light-catchers that humans lack
choices: Their eyes carry special light-catchers that humans lack
Their bodies grow brighter when they pick the right color
They build webs only on flowers of one chosen color
Their footprints leave a glowing stain on bright leaves
context: Some jumping spiders have UV-sensitive cells we lack. Males flash patches that glow only under UV light during their courtship dances.

question: Shine a special blue light on a desert at night and tiny green-blue glowing creatures light up across the sand. What kind of animal is glowing?
answer: Scorpions — their shells glow under ultraviolet light
choices: Scorpions — their shells glow under ultraviolet light
Beetles — their wing cases reflect color in moonlight
Spiders — their eyes shine bright red in headlamps
Worms — their slime trails glow on every desert plant
context: Scorpion shells glow blue-green under UV. The chemical reason is still studied; scientists use UV lamps to find scorpions at night.

question: A tiny creature so small you need a microscope to see it has survived something no other animal can. What did the tardigrade live through?
answer: A trip in open space outside a spaceship
choices: A trip in open space outside a spaceship
A swim through molten lava in a volcano
A walk across the ocean floor at full pressure
A flight inside a tornado for two whole days
context: Tardigrades (water bears) survived ten days exposed to vacuum and radiation on the FOTON-M3 satellite in 2007 — the only animal known to live through open space.

question: A spider's web looks fragile, but the strands are tougher than they seem. Compared to a steel wire of the same thickness, what is spider silk like?
answer: Stronger than steel — pound for pound it's tougher
choices: Stronger than steel — pound for pound it's tougher
Weaker than steel — but stretchier and very soft
Brittle like glass — but quick to make new strands
Heavier than steel — and that is why webs hold weight
context: Spider silk is stronger than steel by weight and tougher than Kevlar. Scientists try to make synthetic versions for body armor.

question: In some forests, billions of large red-eyed insects burst out of the ground all at once — then disappear again for 13 or 17 years. What is going on?
answer: Cicadas — they live underground as nymphs for years
choices: Cicadas — they live underground as nymphs for years
Locusts — they hatch from huge eggs only in dry years
Termites — they come up to swarm once every century
Mayflies — they live a single day then die in the air
context: Periodical cicadas (Magicicada) spend 13 or 17 years underground feeding on tree roots. Both 13 and 17 are prime — likely a defense against predator timing.

question: A praying mantis is a fierce hunter. After two mantises mate, the female sometimes does something startling — what does she do?
answer: She eats the male as her first meal after mating
choices: She eats the male as her first meal after mating
She buries the male alive under a heap of dry leaves
She lays her eggs on the male's back as he runs off
She traps the male inside a silk cocoon for later
context: Female praying mantises sometimes eat the male after — or even during — mating. The protein helps egg production. It's normal mantis biology.

question: A Hercules beetle is the size of your hand. Compared to its tiny body weight, how heavy a thing can this beetle lift?
answer: About 850 times its own weight on its back
choices: About 850 times its own weight on its back
About 5 times its own weight on its back
About 50 times its own weight on its back
About 4,000 times its own weight on its back
context: Hercules beetles can carry roughly 850× their body weight — among the strongest animals known relative to size.

question: Dung beetles roll their ball of food in a perfectly straight line away from the dung pile. On a moonless night with no street lights, what guides them?
answer: Light from the Milky Way galaxy itself
choices: Light from the Milky Way galaxy itself
Smell of the dung pile they just rolled from
Sounds made by other beetles working nearby
Warmth left in the soil from the day's sun
context: Dacke et al. (2013) showed dung beetles navigate by the Milky Way — the only known insect to use it. They orient to the galactic band of light.

question: On tropical islands lives a giant crab as long as your arm. It can crack open coconuts with its claws — and it does something no other crab does. What is it?
answer: It climbs tall palm trees to get coconuts
choices: It climbs tall palm trees to get coconuts
It eats sand grains to grow heavy and stay put
It carries a fish in its claw to lure prey closer
It glows in the dark when the moon comes out
context: The coconut crab (Birgus latro) climbs palm trees, snips coconuts loose, and cracks them open. It's the largest land arthropod alive.

question: When a fish bites a sea cucumber, the sea cucumber does something surprising — it shoots out its own insides at the attacker. What happens next?
answer: It grows new insides and keeps on living
choices: It grows new insides and keeps on living
It dies right after and sinks to the seafloor
It hardens into a shell to protect what is left
It floats up to the surface and waits for help
context: Sea cucumbers eviscerate — they expel sticky internal organs to startle or entangle predators. The lost organs regrow over weeks.

question: A barnacle picks one spot on a rock or whale and stays there its whole life. How does it stick on so firmly that storms can't knock it loose?
answer: It glues itself with a natural cement stronger than super glue
choices: It glues itself with a natural cement stronger than super glue
It drills a deep hole into the rock with its first soft body
It wraps thin rope-like roots around bumps on the surface
It freezes a thin film of cold water under itself as glue
context: Barnacle cement is among the strongest natural adhesives — bonding underwater to anything from rocks to whale skin. Dental scientists study it.

question: An octopus has more hearts than you do. How many hearts pump blood through its body?
answer: Three hearts — two pump gill blood, one pumps the rest
choices: Three hearts — two pump gill blood, one pumps the rest
Two hearts — one for left arms and one for the right
Five hearts — one in the head and one in each of four arms
One huge heart — but it is wrapped around the brain
context: An octopus has three hearts: two branchial hearts pump blood through the gills, one systemic heart pumps it around the body. Its blood is blue (copper-based).

question: A sea star eating a clam does something no person could match — it pushes part of its own body out through its mouth. What part comes out?
answer: Its stomach — it digests the clam outside its body
choices: Its stomach — it digests the clam outside its body
Its lungs — to take in extra oxygen for digestion
Its teeth — sharp ones pop out to drill into the shell
Its tongue — long and sticky to scrape the clam free
context: Sea stars (asteroids) extrude the cardiac stomach through their mouth to digest prey externally. The partly-digested meal is then drawn back inside.

question: Most spiders trap insects in webs. One spider hunts a different way — it swings a sticky ball on a silk thread and catches moths in mid-air. What is it called?
answer: A bolas spider — named for the South American throwing weapon
choices: A bolas spider — named for the South American throwing weapon
A jumping spider — named for its quick leap onto prey
A trapdoor spider — named for its hidden burrow opening
A net-casting spider — named for the web it spreads down
context: Bolas spiders swing a sticky droplet on a thread. They release moth-mimic pheromones so male moths fly close enough to be hit.

question: Some moths are huge — the atlas moth is one of the world's largest. How wide are its wings, tip to tip?
answer: About the length of an adult's hand stretched out — around 25 cm
choices: About the length of an adult's hand stretched out — around 25 cm
About the length of an adult's thumb tip to nail — around 3 cm
About the length of an adult's forearm — around 50 cm
About the length of an adult's full leg — around 80 cm
context: Atlas moths have wingspans up to ~24 cm. As adults they cannot eat — they live a week or two on stored fat from caterpillar days.

question: Big black-and-orange wasps hunt large hairy spiders. The wasp paralyzes the spider with a sting, then drags it to a burrow. What happens to the spider next?
answer: A wasp egg is laid on it and the hatching grub eats the spider
choices: A wasp egg is laid on it and the hatching grub eats the spider
The wasp itself eats the spider whole over many slow weeks
The spider is freed once the wasp builds its own egg case
The spider's web is recycled by the wasp to wrap her young
context: Tarantula hawk wasps paralyze tarantulas and lay one egg on them. The wasp larva eats the spider alive — keeping vital organs for last to keep it fresh.

question: A Portuguese man o' war floats on the ocean with a blue jelly-like top and long stingers below. People often call it a jellyfish — but it isn't. What is it really?
answer: A colony of tiny animals all living together as one body
choices: A colony of tiny animals all living together as one body
A single huge jelly with very long mouth-arms beneath
A type of squid with see-through skin and bright stingers
A floating sea snail that grew a sail from its broken shell
context: A man o' war is a siphonophore — a colony of specialized zooids (float, stingers, digesters, reproducers) that cannot live apart.

question: A garden fills with hundreds of butterflies fluttering together in bright colors. What is this kind of gathering called?
answer: A kaleidoscope of butterflies
choices: A kaleidoscope of butterflies
A flutter of butterflies
A bouquet of butterflies
A carnival of butterflies
context: A group of butterflies is called a kaleidoscope. (Other accepted terms: flight, rabble — but kaleidoscope is the wonder-form.)

question: Pull out the fridge late at night and a dozen cockroaches scatter at once. What is the special name for a group of cockroaches?
answer: An intrusion of cockroaches
choices: An intrusion of cockroaches
A skitter of cockroaches
A creep of cockroaches
A shadow of cockroaches
context: A group of cockroaches is called an intrusion — fittingly descriptive of how you usually encounter them.

question: Camp out on a summer lake at dusk and clouds of biting mosquitoes find you. What word names a large gathering of mosquitoes?
answer: A scourge of mosquitoes
choices: A scourge of mosquitoes
A buzz of mosquitoes
A torment of mosquitoes
A wave of mosquitoes
context: A group of mosquitoes is called a scourge — old language that captured the disease and misery they brought.

question: When billions of locusts darken the sky and strip whole fields bare, what is this gathering traditionally called?
answer: A plague of locusts
choices: A plague of locusts
A tide of locusts
A storm of locusts
A horde of locusts
context: A swarm of locusts is called a plague — the term dates from Biblical Exodus and is still used by entomologists.

question: Some spiders catch insects sitting on the water — and even small fish — by skating across the pond's surface. How do their legs not break through?
answer: Surface tension and water-shedding hairs hold them up
choices: Surface tension and water-shedding hairs hold them up
Tiny air bubbles under each foot puff them up like rafts
Their leg tips are so wide they spread weight like skis
Their bodies are lighter than the water they walk on top of
context: Fishing spiders use surface tension plus hydrophobic leg hairs. Slow-motion video shows them rowing across pond surfaces.

question: A tiny jellyfish off the coast of Italy does something no other animal can — when hurt or starving, it does what?
answer: It turns back into a younger version of itself
choices: It turns back into a younger version of itself
It splits in half and both halves grow brand-new ones
It freezes its body until the danger has passed it by
It glows so brightly that fish are scared right away
context: Turritopsis dohrnii can revert from adult medusa back to polyp stage when stressed — a kind of biological reset. Researchers call it the 'immortal jellyfish.'

question: A type of worm sucks blood from animals and people. Today, hospitals actually buy these worms by the box. Why would a doctor use one?
answer: To keep blood flowing in a reattached finger or ear
choices: To keep blood flowing in a reattached finger or ear
To make a patient feel sleepy before a small surgery
To clean dirt from inside a healing broken-bone cast
To warm up cold hands by drawing blood toward the skin
context: The medicinal leech (Hirudo medicinalis) is FDA-approved. Surgeons use them after reattaching fingers or ears — they keep blood moving while veins reconnect.

question: Humans have raised a special caterpillar for over 5,000 years — it spins a soft thread used to make beautiful cloth. What is the cloth called?
answer: Silk — made from the cocoon thread of the silkworm
choices: Silk — made from the cocoon thread of the silkworm
Wool — made from the hair of a special caterpillar
Cotton — made from the fluff inside the cocoon
Velvet — made from the soft scales on silkworm wings
context: Silk has been made from Bombyx mori cocoons for 5,000+ years (originating in China). Bombyx mori is fully domesticated — it cannot fly or survive in the wild.

question: Bees are not just pretty — almonds, apples, and many other crops need them. About how much of human food depends on bee or other animal pollination?
answer: Roughly one of every three bites you eat
choices: Roughly one of every three bites you eat
Roughly one of every ten bites you eat
Roughly one of every twenty bites you eat
Roughly all the bites you eat each day
context: About a third of human food crops depend on animal pollinators — bees, butterflies, bats, birds. Honeybees alone pollinate California's entire almond crop.

question: The world's largest spider has a leg span as wide as a dinner plate and a body the size of a fist. Despite its scary name, what does it actually eat most often?
answer: Bugs and worms and the occasional small frog or mouse
choices: Bugs and worms and the occasional small frog or mouse
Mostly birds it sneaks up on nests in tree branches
Mostly fish it floats on rivers in the Amazon basin
Mostly fruit pulp from ripe mangoes that fall to the floor
context: Goliath bird-eaters (Theraphosa blondi) rarely eat birds despite the name. They mostly hunt insects, worms, frogs, and the occasional rodent.

question: A bright-red fuzzy 'ant' walks through the desert — but it isn't really an ant at all. Why do people call it the cow killer?
answer: Its sting hurts so badly people say it could kill a cow
choices: Its sting hurts so badly people say it could kill a cow
It crawls into cows' ears and bites them until they fall sick
Its bright color tells cows not to eat the plants nearby
It carries a disease that gives cows a deadly tail rash
context: Velvet ants are actually wingless female wasps. Their sting earns one of the highest pain ratings — hence 'cow killer.' (No cow has ever died from one.)

question: Most ant colonies fight other colonies of the same species. But across thousands of miles of California, southern Europe, and Japan, billions of Argentine ants never attack each other. What does this make their populations?
answer: A single global supercolony — neighbors recognize each other and act as nestmates
choices: A single global supercolony — neighbors recognize each other and act as nestmates
A hormone truce — older queens release scents that block sister colonies from fighting
A loose alliance — they cooperate to hunt but fight when nest space or food turn scarce
Three distinct colonies — they merge once a year for mating then break apart for war
context: Linepithema humile populations on three continents share enough chemical recognition cues that they behave as one supercolony — the largest cooperative society known to biology.

question: Army ants do not build a permanent nest. Each night, they form a living ball of bodies hooked together around the queen and the brood. What is this temporary structure called?
answer: A bivouac — workers link legs to make walls of living ants
choices: A bivouac — workers link legs to make walls of living ants
A spire — workers stack themselves vertically into a small tower
A burrow — workers dig a fresh hole each evening at dusk
A nest — workers hide quickly under rocks before night falls
context: Army ant bivouacs hang from logs or branches. Worker bodies form walls; the queen and brood are inside. By morning the colony marches on. Eciton burchellii is best studied.

question: A bolas spider catches moths by swinging a single sticky bead on a silk line — but the moths fly right to her. Why does the spider catch only male moths and almost no females?
answer: She releases moth pheromone mimics that draw males searching for mates
choices: She releases moth pheromone mimics that draw males searching for mates
Male moths fly more often after dark, while females mostly stay near plants
She times her hunts when only male moths are emerging from their cocoons
Female moths can see the silk thread in the air and stop short of the bola
context: Bolas spiders (Mastophora) release species-specific moth pheromone analogs. Only males drawn to the false 'female' signal arrive — sex-specific lure chemistry.

question: Monarch butterflies migrate up to 3,000 miles from Canada to one valley in Mexico — but no individual monarch lives long enough to make the round trip. How does the population complete it?
answer: Multiple generations relay — migrating great-grandkids find a place they have never seen
choices: Multiple generations relay — migrating great-grandkids find a place they have never seen
Each butterfly hibernates — it resumes the next spring and finishes after four full seasons
Monarchs follow migrating birds — they learn the path from the species ahead of them
One queen lays a scent trail — her short-lived workers follow it on the journey south
context: Monarchs (Danaus plexippus) cycle across 3-4 short-lived summer generations, then one long-lived 'super-generation' migrates south. How they navigate to a place they've never seen is still studied.

question: Hawk moths visit flowers after dark when most colors fade. They still find the right blossoms by seeing something we cannot. What feature lets them choose flowers in low light?
answer: Ultraviolet vision — many flowers reflect UV patterns that act like landing strips to moths
choices: Ultraviolet vision — many flowers reflect UV patterns that act like landing strips to moths
Heat vision — flowers warm up slightly at night and stand out from the cooler leaves nearby
Magnetic vision — moths track flower positions by Earth's magnetic field at fixed angles
Sound echo — moths echolocate the trumpet shape of flowers like little bats in the dark
context: Hawk moths and many other pollinators see UV. Flower 'nectar guides' visible only under UV direct the insect to the right landing spot. Many night flowers reflect UV patterns.

question: In the 1800s, peppered moths in English forests were mostly pale with dark speckles. By 1900, dark forms dominated near coal-burning cities. What changed?
answer: Tree bark blackened with soot, so pale moths now stood out to hungry birds clearly
choices: Tree bark blackened with soot, so pale moths now stood out to hungry birds clearly
Cold winters killed off pale moths' eggs while dark moths' eggs survived due to pigment
Dark moths flew in from a different region and replaced pale moths by out-competing them
Pale moths were caught and pinned by collectors faster than dark moths during this period
context: Peppered moth (Biston betularia) industrial melanism is a textbook case of natural selection. Pollution darkened tree bark; bird predation shifted the population. Clean air laws reversed it.

question: In 1869 a French scientist released some European moths in Massachusetts hoping to start a silk industry. Within decades the moths had defoliated millions of trees. What had gone wrong?
answer: They became an invasive species and their caterpillars ate native trees with no checks
choices: They became an invasive species and their caterpillars ate native trees with no checks
They migrated away from the silk farm and spread north before the scientist could collect
They were wrong color for the silk trade so farmers released them deliberately to fail off
They interbred with native moths and the hybrid offspring stopped making silk altogether
context: Étienne Léopold Trouvelot's 1869 release of European spongy moth (Lymantria dispar, formerly 'gypsy moth') is among the worst entomological accidents in US history. Caterpillars defoliate broadleaf forests.

question: A cuttlefish hovering over a checkered seafloor will, within a second, take on a matching checkerboard pattern of light and dark patches. How does it do this with no brain like ours?
answer: Tiny pigment sacs in its skin called chromatophores expand or pull tight under nerve control
choices: Tiny pigment sacs in its skin called chromatophores expand or pull tight under nerve control
Cold and warm spots in its body shift the color of pigment chemicals dissolved in the blood
Its skin slowly releases ink that floats over the surface and matches whatever lies beneath
Stiff white feathers along its back fan out and rise to copy any shape the cuttlefish sees
context: Cuttlefish (and octopus and squid) skin holds chromatophores — pigment sacs that expand or contract under direct nerve control. Beneath sit reflective iridophores and white leucophores.

question: Garden snails mate by stabbing each other with calcium-carbonate 'darts' before exchanging sperm. The darts don't hurt either snail enough to stop the mating. What is the dart for?
answer: Hormones on the dart help the shooter's sperm survive longer inside the partner's body
choices: Hormones on the dart help the shooter's sperm survive longer inside the partner's body
Calcium from the dart provides nutrition for the baby snails developing in eggs
The dart marks the partner so other snails won't try to mate with it later
The dart breaks the partner's shell open so eggs can develop inside protected
context: Snail 'love darts' carry mucus with hormones that improve the shooter's reproductive success. Both snails are hermaphrodites — both shoot, both receive.

question: Giant clams open their colorful mantles to the sun on coral reefs every day. They do this for the same reason a plant does. What is inside the mantle?
answer: Single-celled algae called zooxanthellae photosynthesize and share food with the clam
choices: Single-celled algae called zooxanthellae photosynthesize and share food with the clam
Tiny shrimp that clean the clam's gills and shed bright pigments as a payment of food
Hot mineral springs of natural sulfur that fuel chemical food production deep within
Microscopic crystals focus sunlight on tiny black-spot eyes embedded in the mantle wall
context: Giant clams (Tridacna) host zooxanthellae — symbiotic dinoflagellates that photosynthesize. The clam grows huge partly because sunlight feeds it through its tenants.

question: A type of sea slug eats algae but doesn't fully digest the chloroplasts inside. The slug keeps the chloroplasts alive in its own skin for months. What does this let the slug do?
answer: It photosynthesizes, and sunlight on its body produces food via stolen chloroplasts
choices: It photosynthesizes, and sunlight on its body produces food via stolen chloroplasts
It glows green at night to startle hungry fish away from its very slow soft body
It grows much faster than other sea slugs because it gets extra mineral nutrition
It heals torn skin in hours by drawing energy directly from the stolen chloroplasts
context: Solar-powered sea slugs (Elysia chlorotica and relatives) practice kleptoplasty — keeping algal chloroplasts alive inside their tissues. They can live months on sunlight alone.

question: A nudibranch grazes on a stinging jellyfish without setting off the stinging cells. The slug then stores the unfired stingers in its own back tips for its own defense. What is this called?
answer: Kleptocnidae — stealing stinging cells from a meal and reusing them as armor
choices: Kleptocnidae — stealing stinging cells from a meal and reusing them as armor
Aposematism — wearing bright colors to warn that the slug itself is poisonous
Mimicry — looking like a stinging jellyfish without having any real defense
Autotomy — dropping body parts when a predator grabs to escape its grip
context: Aeolid nudibranchs eat cnidarian prey and shunt undischarged nematocysts to dorsal cerata. Touch the slug — and the stolen stingers fire. A genuine kleptocnidae system.

question: Spring rains fill a dry depression in the desert and within days the pool is full of swimming shrimp. The pool was bone dry for two years. Where did the shrimp come from?
answer: Eggs in the dirt — fairy shrimp eggs can stay alive for decades through dry years
choices: Eggs in the dirt — fairy shrimp eggs can stay alive for decades through dry years
Eggs in the wind — passing storms blew the shrimp eggs in from another pool nearby
Eggs on birds — wading birds carried eggs on their feet from distant wetter ponds
Eggs in mud — mud washed in from a faraway river carried the eggs in this season
context: Fairy shrimp produce cysts — dormant eggs that survive years of drying. When ephemeral pools fill, the cysts hatch within days. A built-in time machine.

question: A big new shell washes up on the beach. Within minutes, hermit crabs line up by size. The biggest crab takes the new shell — then what happens next?
answer: The next-biggest takes the old shell of the biggest, and so on down a chain of crabs
choices: The next-biggest takes the old shell of the biggest, and so on down a chain of crabs
The other crabs leave and find their own shells elsewhere alone on the wider beach
All the other crabs at once fight one another for the newly abandoned older shells
The biggest crab returns to its old shell, and the new one is left for short visits
context: Hermit crabs form 'vacancy chains' — when one moves to a new shell, the next size down moves into its old one, on down the line. Studied by Briffa and others.

question: Coconut crabs crack open whole coconuts with their claws. Lab tests of pinching force show that pound for pound, a coconut crab's claw is among the strongest grips of any animal. What does it match?
answer: The bite of a lion — even though the crab weighs only about four kilograms
choices: The bite of a lion — even though the crab weighs only about four kilograms
The bite of a goldfish — surprisingly weak for an animal that size
The grip of a chimpanzee's hand — but only for very brief pinches
The crush of a python's coiled body — when measured over a one-second test
context: Oka et al. (2016) measured coconut crab pinching forces up to ~3,300 newtons — matching lion bite force. The strongest pinch among arthropods alive.

question: A large gray-and-yellow moth with a skull pattern on its back flies into a beehive at night. The bees do not attack it. What is the moth doing — and why does it get away?
answer: Stealing honey — it makes a chemical bees mistake for one of their own
choices: Stealing honey — it makes a chemical bees mistake for one of their own
Mating with the queen — the bees treat it like a new candidate drone
Laying eggs in cells — it lays eggs that worker bees raise as their own
Cooling the hive — its rapid wingbeats fan the cells like the bees do
context: The death's-head hawkmoth (Acherontia) raids beehives for honey. It produces chemical signals (mimicking bee odor) and emits squeaks that may dampen bee aggression.

question: An old lobster doesn't slow down the way an old dog or old human does. It keeps growing and laying eggs at the same rate. What finally causes most lobsters to die?
answer: Molting failure — they can't shed the old shell as they get larger and exhaustion sets in
choices: Molting failure — they can't shed the old shell as they get larger and exhaustion sets in
Memory loss — they forget where their den is and starve searching for the right cave
Heart failure — their three hearts wear out at the same time as other organs do
Cancer — old lobsters get tumors at high rates compared to other crustacean species
context: Lobsters show 'negligible senescence' — they don't age in the typical sense. Most die from being unable to molt successfully as they grow ever larger.

question: Deep-sea worms live in tubes attached to hydrothermal vents. The tail end of the worm sits in water that is over 80°C — hot enough to cook an egg. What lets the worm survive?
answer: Heat-tolerant bacteria coat its back, releasing heat-shock proteins that stabilize the worm's cells
choices: Heat-tolerant bacteria coat its back, releasing heat-shock proteins that stabilize the worm's cells
It pumps cold water through its tube from above, washing the hot vent water away constantly
It produces a thick mucus layer around its body that drops the temperature it actually feels
It can spend most of its day with its tail tucked away from the hottest part of the vent water
context: Alvinella pompejana — the Pompeii worm — has bacterial mat coating its back. The bacteria produce protective chemicals; the worm tolerates one of the largest temperature gradients known in any animal.

question: Orb-weaver spiders make a new web every single morning. They tear down the old one, roll up the silk, and eat it. Why eat your own web?
answer: The silk proteins are expensive to make, so recycling saves energy and amino acids
choices: The silk proteins are expensive to make, so recycling saves energy and amino acids
Old silk smells like the spider and lets ants follow the trail back to her hideout
Sunlight breaks down old silk and the spider eats it before broken strands harm her
Old silk attracts mites that would crawl up into the spider's mouth as she sleeps
context: Many orb-weavers consume old silk and recycle the protein into new silk. Silk synthesis is metabolically expensive; the worn-out web is too valuable to throw away.

question: A trapdoor spider digs a vertical hole and covers it with a silk-hinged lid. A beetle walks by — and the spider flies out, grabs the beetle, and slams the door shut. How does the spider know to strike?
answer: Silk trip lines from the door pick up footstep vibrations that signal prey above
choices: Silk trip lines from the door pick up footstep vibrations that signal prey above
Light from above flickers when an animal walks by and the spider's eyes catch this
The spider listens for the heartbeat of prey through the ground from in the burrow
The lid acts as a magnetic compass and senses tiny metal in the prey's exoskeleton
context: Trapdoor spiders set silk 'trip lines' radiating from the door. A footstep on a trip line is the cue. The spider lunges out and snatches prey from above with millisecond timing.

question: A male peacock spider — smaller than a grain of rice — courts a female by raising bright fan-like flaps on his back and waving his legs in a precise rhythm. What happens if he gets the dance wrong?
answer: The female eats him — wrong species or wrong rhythm and she treats him as prey
choices: The female eats him — wrong species or wrong rhythm and she treats him as prey
She walks away — he just gets one more try on a different day next week
She mates with him anyway — the dance is for show only, with no real test
She covers his eyes — and waits while he tries the dance over and over again
context: Peacock spider (Maratus) males perform species-specific dances. The female judges; wrong species or poor performance and he's prey, not mate. Otto and Hill have documented dozens of species.

question: A Goliath bird-eater spider is the size of a dinner plate. When threatened, it doesn't bite first — it rubs its back legs together and sends tiny barbed hairs flying. What do the hairs do?
answer: They irritate the eyes and skin of the attacker enough to drive most predators away
choices: They irritate the eyes and skin of the attacker enough to drive most predators away
They cling to the air and float up into clouds to confuse a circling predator
They release a sticky glue that traps the attacker's feet until it gives up trying
They mimic a wasp sting by injecting a numbing venom into any skin they touch
context: New World tarantulas like Theraphosa kick urticating hairs from their abdomens. The barbed hairs irritate eyes, skin, and lungs. Cheaper than venom and works on big mammals.

question: A velvet worm — a soft, ancient relative of arthropods — hunts at night in tropical rainforests. When it spots prey or a threat, it fires sticky strings from cannons on its head. How does it aim?
answer: It sweeps the head left and right, painting a wide spray of glue onto the target zone
choices: It sweeps the head left and right, painting a wide spray of glue onto the target zone
It uses heat sensors to lock its head exactly on the prey's body and fires once square
It releases scent that draws the prey close to its mouth, where short claws then strike
It hooks tiny silk lines onto the prey first and reels in before any glue is needed at all
context: Onychophorans (velvet worms) spray slime from oral papillae. They sweep the head, painting prey or threats with a sticky web. Velvet worms are a living-fossil phylum dating from the Cambrian.

question: A bombardier beetle's defensive spray reaches near 100°C and shoots out in rapid pulses, not a steady stream. The pulses make the spray more effective. Why does the pulsing matter?
answer: Pulses give the chamber time to cool between bursts, letting the beetle fire many times
choices: Pulses give the chamber time to cool between bursts, letting the beetle fire many times
Pulses sound louder than a steady stream and scare away most birds before any contact
Pulses paint a wider area than steady spray and catch any attacker even at distance away
Pulses make the spray look bigger to predators since each puff seems like a new burst
context: High-speed imaging (Aneshansley & Eisner) shows the beetle fires ~500 pulses per second. The pulsing prevents heat damage to the beetle's own chamber while extending the firing range.

question: Of all animals on Earth, one kills more humans than any other — about 700,000 people per year. Which is it?
answer: Mosquitoes — they carry malaria, dengue, yellow fever, and other diseases
choices: Mosquitoes — they carry malaria, dengue, yellow fever, and other diseases
Crocodiles — they attack thousands of fishermen on tropical rivers each year
Sharks — they attack swimmers in coastal waters across all warm oceans
Hippos — they kill more people than any other large animal in Africa
context: Mosquitoes are the deadliest 'animal' to humans — vectors of malaria (~600,000 deaths/year), dengue, yellow fever, Zika, West Nile. Disease transmission, not direct attack.

question: Comb jellies are nearly transparent ocean drifters. As they pulse along, their eight comb-rows scatter light into shimmering rainbow colors. Are the colors actually pigments?
answer: No — the colors come from the comb rows splitting white light like a prism, not from pigment
choices: No — the colors come from the comb rows splitting white light like a prism, not from pigment
Yes — pigments along the comb rows turn pink in cold water and blue in warm water
Yes — and the colors fade after the comb jelly dies and the pigments break down quickly
No — the colors are made by glowing bacteria living inside the comb rows of these animals
context: The rainbow shimmer on a comb jelly (ctenophore) is structural — light diffracts off the moving comb rows (cilia). No pigment. Comb jellies are NOT true jellyfish.

question: A six-foot worm buried in the seafloor with only its jaws showing snaps a passing fish in half with one strike. What family does this monster belong to?
answer: Polychaete worms — segmented bristleworms, distantly related to earthworms above
choices: Polychaete worms — segmented bristleworms, distantly related to earthworms above
Flatworms — simple unsegmented worms that swim through ocean water columns
Roundworms — the most abundant animal on Earth but mostly tiny in body size
Ribbon worms — long flat-bodied predators that grow to similar lengths underwater
context: The bobbit worm (Eunice aphroditois) is a polychaete — segmented worms. Five spring-loaded jaws on a hidden body up to 3 m long. Strikes are faster than the eye can follow.

question: A vinegaroon looks like a scorpion with no stinger. When a predator approaches it lifts its tail end and sprays a clear liquid that smells of vinegar. What is the liquid actually made of?
answer: Concentrated acetic acid — the same acid in kitchen vinegar but at much higher strength
choices: Concentrated acetic acid — the same acid in kitchen vinegar but at much higher strength
Sulfuric acid — at strengths similar to a chemistry lab supply for routine etching
Hydrochloric acid — strong enough to dissolve any softshell predator close up to one
Formic acid — the acid found in ant venom but at higher concentrations than ants make
context: Vinegaroons (Thelyphonida) spray ~85% acetic acid laced with caprylic acid. The vinegar smell carries; the spray irritates eyes and mucous membranes of would-be predators.

question: Paper wasps build hanging gray-and-tan nests with thin walls that look surprisingly like paper. The resemblance isn't a coincidence — what is the wasp's nest material?
answer: Chewed wood fibers mixed with wasp saliva, so wasps invented paper before humans
choices: Chewed wood fibers mixed with wasp saliva, so wasps invented paper before humans
Dried mud rolled into thin sheets and bonded with wasp saliva for a hard texture
Spider silk gathered from old webs and woven into thin layered walls by wasp jaws
Wax made in glands on the wasp's abdomen, like the comb that honeybees construct
context: Paper wasps (Polistes and others) chew wood fibers and mix them with saliva. The pulp dries into a paper that holds up to weather. Humans copied the chemistry millennia later.

question: Luna moths have long, twisted tails on their hind wings. When bats hunt them by echolocation, the bats' clicks often hit the tails instead of the body. What does this prove?
answer: The tails act as acoustic decoys — bat sonar reflects off them, not the moth's body
choices: The tails act as acoustic decoys — bat sonar reflects off them, not the moth's body
The tails act as gliders — they slow the moth down enough that bats often overshoot
The tails act as sound-makers — emitting a high frequency that jams bat sonar mid-strike
The tails act as poison delivery — biting bats get a mouthful of irritating chemical
context: Barber et al. (PNAS, 2015) showed luna moth tails confuse bat echolocation — the spinning tails reflect a stronger signal than the body, drawing the strike away. Acoustic decoy evolved.

question: Open a window and a swarm of flies seems to push in. What term for a group of flies appears in old English collective-noun lists?
answer: A business of flies
choices: A business of flies
A nuisance of flies
A buzz of flies
A storm of flies
context: A group of flies is called a 'business' — from medieval terms of venery. The list also accepts 'swarm' but 'business' is the wonder-form.

question: Monarchs spending winter in their Mexican mountain valley pack so densely on fir trees that the branches sag under their weight. What name fits this kind of overwintering group?
answer: A cluster of butterflies
choices: A cluster of butterflies
A bouquet of butterflies
A canopy of butterflies
A drift of butterflies
context: Overwintering monarchs cluster on oyamel firs in Michoacán. Cluster is the term ecologists use; kaleidoscope refers to flying groups.

question: Honeybees, ants, and termites all live in colonies with one reproducing queen and many sterile workers. Yet ants and bees are related; termites are distantly related cockroaches. What does this pattern suggest about eusocial life?
answer: Convergent evolution — the same social structure evolved separately in different insect lineages because it pays off
choices: Convergent evolution — the same social structure evolved separately in different insect lineages because it pays off
Single origin — all colonial insects share one common ancestor and inherited social life from that one source
Parallel hybrid lines — termites and ants interbred long ago, leaving social genes in both modern lineages
Cold-climate response — colonies formed only after the ice ages forced insects to share heat in tight groups
context: Eusociality has evolved at least a dozen times in arthropods alone — honeybees and ants share recent ancestry, but termites independently evolved similar social structure from cockroach-like ancestors. Convergent solution to similar selection pressures.

question: Bees, ants, and wasps share a strange genetic system: fertilized eggs become females (workers, queen), unfertilized eggs become males (drones). What does this asymmetry produce?
