answer: Sisters share 75% of their genes — closer than they would be to their own daughters
choices: Sisters share 75% of their genes — closer than they would be to their own daughters
Sons inherit only the father's genes — never any mix from both parents at all
All workers in a hive are genetic clones — every worker is genetically identical
Males have twice the chromosomes of females — and grow much larger as a result
context: Hymenopteran haplodiploidy: males are haploid (one set), females diploid (two sets). Hamilton showed full sisters share ~0.75 of their genes — more than they'd share with daughters (0.5). A push toward worker altruism.

question: Leafcutter ants face a constant threat: another fungus called Escovopsis tries to overgrow the colony's fungus garden. The ants prevent this by carrying a third partner on their bodies. What is the third partner?
answer: Bacteria — they grow on the ants' skin and produce antibiotics that kill Escovopsis
choices: Bacteria — they grow on the ants' skin and produce antibiotics that kill Escovopsis
Mites — they hunt down Escovopsis spores on the garden walls and eat them
Pollen — the ants leave it on the garden to confuse Escovopsis chemical signals
Plant resins — ants gather drops from leaves and paint them around the chamber
context: Currie et al. (1999, 2003) showed leafcutter ants carry Pseudonocardia bacteria on cuticles. The bacteria produce antifungals that suppress the Escovopsis parasite. A four-way symbiosis: ant + fungus + bacterium + parasite.

question: Eusociality means colony life with one breeder and many sterile helpers. This system is iconic in bees and ants. What unusual mammal also lives this way?
answer: Naked mole rats — underground rodent colonies have one breeding queen and sterile workers
choices: Naked mole rats — underground rodent colonies have one breeding queen and sterile workers
Vampire bats — their colonies have one female who breeds and many helpers underground
Meerkats — all members of a troop are sterile except one breeding pair on the surface
Beavers — only the dominant pair breeds and the rest help raise the kits and dam
context: Naked mole rats (Heterocephalus glaber) are one of two known eusocial mammals (Damaraland mole rats are the other). Sherman, Jarvis, Alexander (1991) documented the structure. A cross-class echo of the insect pattern.

question: A sea slug eats algae but instead of fully digesting the chloroplasts, it stores them functional in its own tissues for weeks to months. The slug can then live on sunlight. What is the technical name for this trick?
answer: Kleptoplasty — keeping chloroplasts alive in cells where they would not normally survive
choices: Kleptoplasty — keeping chloroplasts alive in cells where they would not normally survive
Symbiosis — both partners benefit and stay in physical contact throughout the slug's life
Endocytosis — the slug pulls algae into vacuoles to digest them slowly over weeks
Apoptosis — chloroplasts trigger programmed cell death of digestive cells slowly
context: Kleptoplasty: 'stolen plastids.' The chloroplasts continue to photosynthesize in foreign cells without the algal nucleus that normally maintains them. Elysia chlorotica is the best-studied case.

question: Cleaner shrimp on coral reefs set up stations where moray eels and groupers — predators — come to be cleaned of parasites. The shrimp climb into the predator's mouth and emerge unharmed. What does this prove about reef ecology?
answer: Mutualism crosses prey-predator lines because when both sides benefit, hunters respect a truce
choices: Mutualism crosses prey-predator lines because when both sides benefit, hunters respect a truce
Cleaner shrimp produce a venom that paralyzes the moray's bite reflex during a cleaning visit
Morays only cooperate with cleaners they have known since juvenile life on the very same reef
Cleaner shrimp move slowly enough that morays cannot register them as prey moving in to eat
context: Cleaner shrimp (Lysmata, Stenopus) and cleaner wrasse run a stable mutualism on most reefs. Clients line up; cleaners eat parasites and dead skin. Trust holds across encounters — neither side defects.

question: Barnacles cannot move once they cement to a rock. Yet they reproduce sexually with neighbors that may be inches away. They solve this with an unusual anatomical feature — what is it?
answer: Longest penis-to-body ratio of any animal, up to eight times body length to reach neighbors
choices: Longest penis-to-body ratio of any animal, up to eight times body length to reach neighbors
They release sperm into the water and currents drift it toward another barnacle in the patch
They release eggs that float free until another barnacle's water currents pull them in for fertilizing
They reproduce asexually by splitting once a year and produce identical clones around themselves
context: Acorn barnacles (Balanus and others) have penises up to ~8× their body length — the longest body-relative ratio of any animal. The trade-off: when the neighbors are far, the penis grows longer.

question: When a sea cucumber is severely threatened, it does more than evert its stomach — some species shoot out a tangle of sticky white tubes from their backside that entangle the attacker. What are these tubes?
answer: Cuvierian tubules — sticky internal threads ejected as defense, then regenerated
choices: Cuvierian tubules — sticky internal threads ejected as defense, then regenerated
Tube feet — normally used for movement, repurposed in emergencies as glue threads
Stomach lining — the same tissue the cucumber everts but rolled into tube shapes
Gill threads — used to extract oxygen normally, made sticky on contact with seawater
context: Cuvierian tubules: dedicated defensive threads from the cloaca. They swell in seawater into a sticky glue. Some species can fire them at small predators meters away. The cucumber regenerates them over weeks.

question: A small barnacle larva finds a crab, injects itself through a joint, and grows a network inside the crab's body. It eventually emerges from the crab's underside as an egg sac. What has it done to the crab?
answer: Castrated the crab and forced it to care for the parasite's eggs as if they were its own
choices: Castrated the crab and forced it to care for the parasite's eggs as if they were its own
Killed the crab from inside while still using its outer shell as a moving home for travel
Cloned the crab, turning it into a copy of the parasite that the original lays as eggs
Replaced the crab's brain with the parasite's nerves, controlling crab movement directly
context: Sacculina barnacles parasitize crabs — castrating them, redirecting their grooming behavior, and using the crab's body as host. The crab grooms the parasite's egg sac as if it were its own brood. A genuinely alien manipulation.

question: A single-celled parasite can only reproduce inside a cat. To get there, it manipulates the behavior of its intermediate host — a rat. What change does the parasite cause?
answer: Infected rats lose fear of cat odor and investigate it instead of fleeing, getting eaten
choices: Infected rats lose fear of cat odor and investigate it instead of fleeing, getting eaten
Infected rats become hyperactive and exhaust themselves until they collapse near cat dens
Infected rats grow brighter fur that catches a cat's eye at lower light levels in evenings
Infected rats produce stronger urine scents that attract cats from longer ranges across the yard
context: Toxoplasma gondii reverses rat fear of cat odor. Berdoy et al. (2000) showed infected rats are attracted to cat urine. The parasite needs a cat host to complete its life cycle.

question: A hair-thin worm spends its juvenile life inside a cricket. When ready to reproduce, it makes the cricket do something the cricket would never do — what?
answer: Jump into water and drown — the worm needs water to mate and lay eggs
choices: Jump into water and drown — the worm needs water to mate and lay eggs
Climb to the highest tree branch — exposing the cricket to a quick bird strike
Stop singing — silencing predators' attention so the worm can emerge unseen
Eat its own legs off — releasing the worm faster from a more rigid body
context: Horsehair worms (Nematomorpha) inhabit crickets, manipulate the host to seek water, then emerge in the water to mate. Thomas et al. (Nature, 2002) documented the protein-driven behavior change.

question: A fungus infects an ant in a tropical rainforest. The fungus makes the ant climb a leaf, bite the central vein, and lock its jaws. The ant then dies in that exact position — and a fungus stalk grows from the ant's head. Why this precise position?
answer: Leaf height and humidity at that spot are optimal for the fungus to release spores onto ants below
choices: Leaf height and humidity at that spot are optimal for the fungus to release spores onto ants below
The bite traps the ant in a place where bird predators can find it most easily for the fungus's gain
The position is random; the ant happens to die at the spot where the climbing instinct stops working
The leaf releases chemicals the fungus needs to mature inside the ant's head over the next few weeks
context: Ophiocordyceps unilateralis (carpenter ant) — Hughes et al. (2011) showed the fungus drives precise leaf-position behavior. Ant clamps the leaf vein at fungus-optimal humidity height. A 'death grip.'

question: Insects, spiders, crabs, and lobsters all wear an exoskeleton made of the same material. What molecule do they share?
answer: Chitin — a tough polysaccharide that also makes up fungal cell walls and squid beaks
choices: Chitin — a tough polysaccharide that also makes up fungal cell walls and squid beaks
Keratin — the protein that makes hair, nails, and the scales of pangolins and birds
Cellulose — the structural sugar in wood and most plant cell walls everywhere
Calcium phosphate — the mineral in vertebrate bones and the shells of mollusks too
context: Chitin is the universal arthropod exoskeleton. The same polymer turns up in fungal walls and the beaks of cephalopods — chitin spans kingdoms with surprising structural reach.

question: Comb jellies look like jellyfish but are evolutionarily distinct. Some recent genetic studies have suggested they may be the sister group to all other animals — older than sponges in the lineage. What would this mean if true?
answer: Either the nervous system evolved twice, or sponges lost theirs — a major rewrite of animal origins
choices: Either the nervous system evolved twice, or sponges lost theirs — a major rewrite of animal origins
Animals likely evolved on land before moving into the sea — reversing the standard textbook story
All modern animals descend directly from comb jellies — wiping out cnidarians from the tree
Comb jellies are not really animals at all but something else — close to plants or fungi
context: Dunn et al. (2008), Ryan et al. (2013), Whelan et al. (2017) found comb jellies (Ctenophora) sister to all other animals in some analyses. This forces either independent nervous-system evolution in cnidarians/bilaterians or loss in sponges. Active phylogenomic debate.

question: Tardigrades survive vacuum, radiation, and temperatures from −272°C to 150°C. They do this by entering a special dried-out state. What is this state called?
answer: Cryptobiosis — metabolism nearly halts, water is replaced by a sugar called trehalose for protection
choices: Cryptobiosis — metabolism nearly halts, water is replaced by a sugar called trehalose for protection
Hibernation — they sleep deeply but at body temperatures only a few degrees below normal
Estivation — they survive dry summer conditions by burrowing underground in a cool spot
Diapause — they pause development between life stages for short, predictable seasonal windows
context: Tardigrade cryptobiosis: 99%+ of body water is replaced by trehalose and damage-suppressor proteins (CAHS, Dsup). Metabolism drops below detection limits. They can be rehydrated decades later and resume.

question: When Argentine ants invade a Mediterranean ecosystem, they outcompete native ants. Within years, lizard populations also drop. Which mechanism best explains the lizard decline?
answer: Lizards depend on native ant species for food, and Argentine ants displace them so lizards lose prey
choices: Lizards depend on native ant species for food, and Argentine ants displace them so lizards lose prey
Argentine ants directly attack and kill larger lizards by swarming them in numbers each spring season
Argentine ants carry a disease specific to lizards that wipes out their adult breeding populations
Argentine ant pheromones disrupt lizard scent-marking and prevent any successful mating each season
context: Suarez et al. and others documented horned-lizard declines following Argentine ant invasion of southern California. Native harvester ants are the lizards' main food; Argentine ants outcompete harvesters without being acceptable prey themselves.

question: If every other animal on Earth disappeared, you could still see the world's basic shape — outlines of forests, soil, rivers, oceans — because of where one group of animals lives. Which group?
answer: Nematodes — roundworms that live in nearly every habitat from soil to deep sea
choices: Nematodes — roundworms that live in nearly every habitat from soil to deep sea
Insects — they outnumber other animal groups in terrestrial habitats and species
Mites — they live on virtually every surface but most are microscopic in size
Springtails — tiny soil arthropods cover most forest floors in great numbers
context: Nematodes outnumber every other animal — estimated 4 of every 5 animals on Earth are nematodes. N.A. Cobb's 1914 famous passage about seeing 'ghosts of nematodes' tracing every river, plant, and city.

question: A marine worm hatches as a tiny larva with no sex. If it lands on bare rock, it becomes a centimeter-long female. If it lands on another female, it becomes a tiny dwarf male inside her. What determines sex here?
answer: Environmental cue from the substrate — landing site decides sex through chemical signals
choices: Environmental cue from the substrate — landing site decides sex through chemical signals
Genetics alone — the larva already has its sex chromosomes; substrate just triggers growth
Temperature of the water column — where the larva first sinks down decides sex on contact
Egg yolk reserves at hatching — better-fed larvae become females, smaller ones become males
context: Bonellia viridis (green spoonworm) — the female's proboscis releases bonellin, which masculinizes any larva that contacts it. Larvae that land on rock develop as females. One of the cleanest cases of environmental sex determination.

question: After the Clean Air Acts of 1956 (UK) and 1970 (US) reduced industrial soot, peppered moth populations shifted again. The dark forms declined and pale forms recovered. What does the reversibility prove about natural selection?
answer: Selection has no direction — when pressure reverses, the population shifts back to the now-matching form
choices: Selection has no direction — when pressure reverses, the population shifts back to the now-matching form
Dark moths permanently changed and could not switch back — only new pale mutations restored a balance
Pollution selected only on adults — moth eggs were unaffected by the soot all along the whole cycle
Climate change, not pollution, was the real driver — and climate has not reversed since these laws
context: Cook & Saccheri reviewed the post-1970 recovery: as bark lichens regrew and bark lightened, bird predation reversed the selection pressure. Allele frequencies shifted back. Natural selection is direction-following, not goal-directed.

question: In Africa, large termite mounds rise out of grasslands like cathedrals. Inside, the termites tend a fungus garden — separately evolved from the leafcutter ants' fungus farms. What does the parallel suggest?
answer: Convergent agriculture — insects independently invented fungus farming on different continents
choices: Convergent agriculture — insects independently invented fungus farming on different continents
A shared ancestor — termites and ants both inherited fungus farming from a common original
Co-evolution with the same fungus — Termitomyces is the only fungus social insects can grow
Cultural learning — termites learned the trick from ants over millions of years of overlap
context: Macrotermitinae termites in Africa farm Termitomyces fungi inside mounds; leafcutter ants in the Americas farm Leucoagaricus. Independent origins of fungiculture in insects — convergent agricultural evolution.

question: Fairy shrimp cysts can survive being dried for decades, frozen, or even passing through a duck's gut. What does this suite of survival features allow the species to do over time?
answer: Track unpredictable wet years and disperse across continents via animals and dust storms
choices: Track unpredictable wet years and disperse across continents via animals and dust storms
Predict rainfall years in advance by sensing barometric pressure shifts in the cyst
Time hatching to lunar cycles for synchronized breeding across all desert pools
Avoid all competition by hatching only in pools where no other crustaceans have lived
context: Fairy shrimp (Anostraca) bet-hedge: cysts hatch in some wet seasons, stay dormant in others. The 'egg bank' tolerates years of unpredictability. Dispersal via ducks and dust is well documented.

question: A coral reef looks like a colorful undersea garden — but coral is not a plant. What kind of animal is each coral polyp most closely related to?
answer: Jellyfish — both are cnidarians with stinging cells and radial symmetry in body plan
choices: Jellyfish — both are cnidarians with stinging cells and radial symmetry in body plan
Sponges — both are simple filter feeders that anchor to the seafloor for life as adults
Sea stars — both have radial symmetry and tube feet on the bottom of the body
Sea cucumbers — both are echinoderms that anchor and filter water for plankton
context: Coral polyps are anthozoan cnidarians — sister to jellyfish and sea anemones. The reef structure is calcium carbonate skeletons of countless polyps. Each polyp houses zooxanthellae (algae) that photosynthesize.

question: Male Hercules beetles grow enormous head horns used in fights with other males over mates. Larger horns mean more wins — but they cost the larvae months of extra growth. What does this trade-off illustrate?
answer: Sexual selection — a trait costly to the carrier can spread if it improves mating success enough
choices: Sexual selection — a trait costly to the carrier can spread if it improves mating success enough
Genetic drift — random changes in small beetle populations slowly favor larger horns over time
Founder effect — early colonizers happened to have large horns and the population kept them
Coevolution — male and female horns track each other in a shared evolutionary arms race
context: Sexual selection (Darwin, 1871) — costly ornaments and weapons spread when they raise reproductive success. Dynastes hercules horns: Emlen's lab models show the cost-benefit threshold. Females rarely have horns.

question: A small leafhopper imported to California in the 1990s spread a deadly bacterial disease through grapevines and citrus groves. What was the leafhopper actually doing as it moved between plants?
answer: Carrying Xylella bacteria in its mouth from infected to healthy plants while feeding
choices: Carrying Xylella bacteria in its mouth from infected to healthy plants while feeding
Eating grape leaves so quickly that vines died from defoliation in two seasons
Releasing a venom that withered vines on first contact during summer feeding
Laying eggs that hatched into grape-killing caterpillars at every visit
context: Homalodisca vitripennis (glassy-winged sharpshooter) vectors Xylella fastidiosa — causes Pierce's disease in grapes, citrus variegated chlorosis. A textbook vector-borne plant disease.

question: On a few precisely timed nights each year, an entire coral reef releases eggs and sperm into the water at once — a blizzard of pink-and-white bundles. What synchronizes the release across square miles?
answer: Moonlight cycles — corals time spawning to specific phases of the moon plus water temperature
choices: Moonlight cycles — corals time spawning to specific phases of the moon plus water temperature
Chemical signals — a few keystone polyps fire pheromones that cascade across the reef in an hour
Daylight readings — corals time spawning to a precise sunrise reading using light-sensing cells
Salinity drops — corals only spawn when rainfall raises freshwater levels above the reef surface
context: Mass coral spawning on the Great Barrier Reef synchronizes to full moon + water temperature + dusk timing. Harrison et al. (1984) first documented; the cue cocktail keeps spawning across a reef within minutes.

question: Some orb weavers add bright zig-zag silk patterns called stabilimenta to their webs. The function is debated. Which is NOT a hypothesis researchers seriously test?
answer: The pattern releases attractant pheromone — most studies focus on visual cues, not chemical ones
choices: The pattern releases attractant pheromone — most studies focus on visual cues, not chemical ones
The pattern is visible to large animals — it warns them not to walk through the web by accident
The pattern attracts prey by reflecting ultraviolet light — similar to flower nectar guides do
The pattern hides the spider — it breaks up its outline against the web's geometric center spot
context: Stabilimentum function is genuinely open. Three live hypotheses: warning, prey attraction (UV), camouflage. Pheromone-attractant is not a leading hypothesis — research focuses on visual cues.

question: A vinegaroon's defensive acetic-acid spray can reach 80 cm. Predators learn to leave them alone after one encounter. What does this defensive strategy demonstrate?
answer: Aposematism — the vinegar smell becomes a learned warning signal across predator generations
choices: Aposematism — the vinegar smell becomes a learned warning signal across predator generations
Müllerian mimicry — vinegaroons resemble scorpions and benefit from scorpion-warning learning
Batesian mimicry — vinegaroons look dangerous but actually have no defense beyond bluffing
Crypsis — the spray works only when the vinegaroon is hidden first, never in open combat
context: Aposematism = honest warning signal. The vinegaroon's vinegar smell becomes a predator-learned cue: 'don't bite this.' Learning shifts the cost-benefit for future encounters. Other predators may pick up similar lessons.

question: A tarantula doesn't have lungs like ours. It has paired structures called 'book lungs' on its underside. Why the name?
answer: Inside each is a stack of thin plates like pages of a book, and gas exchanges across the plate surfaces
choices: Inside each is a stack of thin plates like pages of a book, and gas exchanges across the plate surfaces
The Latin word for breath shares a root with the Latin word for book due to historical word borrowing
Spiders that lost book lungs evolved into bookworms, and the old nickname stuck across many centuries
Book-lung is the English mistranslation of an Arabic word for a small woven mat used in old prayer day
context: Book lungs: thin stacked lamellae like pages of a book. Hemolymph circulates through the plates; air enters through a slit (spiracle). The design dates back to early Paleozoic chelicerates.

question: A jewel wasp stings a much larger cockroach not once but twice. The first sting paralyzes the legs briefly. The second sting is the precise one. Where does it land?
answer: The cockroach's brain — and the wasp finds the exact spot every time without sight
choices: The cockroach's brain — and the wasp finds the exact spot every time without sight
The cockroach's heart — slowing the circulation enough to keep it groggy but alive
The cockroach's thorax — paralyzing the wings only and leaving legs working normally
The cockroach's abdomen — releasing pheromones that make the cockroach passive
context: Ampulex compressa's second sting targets the subesophageal ganglion — a specific cluster in the brain. The wasp uses sensory feedback from her stinger; needles probe until the chemical landscape matches. Libersat's lab mapped the targeting.

question: Giant tube worms grow over a meter long at hydrothermal vents and have no mouth, gut, or anus. They survive entirely on what their internal bacteria produce. What energy source do the bacteria use?
answer: Hydrogen sulfide from vent water — they oxidize it to make sugars in chemosynthesis
choices: Hydrogen sulfide from vent water — they oxidize it to make sugars in chemosynthesis
Sunlight from above — reaching the vents indirectly through the clear water column
Methane from sediments — a different chemosynthetic pathway than sulfide oxidation
Electricity from microbes — direct electron transfer through fuel cells powers growth
context: Riftia pachyptila chemosynthesis: symbiotic bacteria in the trophosome oxidize H2S to fix CO2. The worm has hemoglobin that binds both O2 and H2S — fueling the bacteria. Cavanaugh et al. (1981) discovered the partnership.

question: Darwin saw a Madagascar orchid with a 30-cm nectar tube. He predicted a hawkmoth with a tongue of matching length must exist. Decades after his death, the moth was found. What does this case demonstrate?
answer: Coevolution — flower and pollinator can lock into a mutual arms race over very long timescales
choices: Coevolution — flower and pollinator can lock into a mutual arms race over very long timescales
Convergent evolution — unrelated moths independently evolved long tongues for similar reasons
Genetic drift — the orchid happened to evolve a long tube without any matching pollinator
Sexual selection — female orchids choose mates with the longest tubes for breeding success
context: Xanthopan morganii praedicta — named for Darwin's prediction. Pollinator of Angraecum sesquipedale, the Madagascar star orchid. Coevolution of corolla tube length and proboscis length. Wallace also predicted it.

question: A leaf is mostly cellulose — a tough sugar most animals cannot digest. Caterpillars that live on leaves get past this by relying on what?
answer: Gut microbes that break cellulose down — enough for the caterpillar to absorb the sugar from leaves
choices: Gut microbes that break cellulose down — enough for the caterpillar to absorb the sugar from leaves
An enzyme they synthesize themselves called cellulase — similar to that fungi make on their own
Dissolving leaves in a strong acid in their gut — similar to what mammals do for meat in stomach
Eating only the soft pulp inside thick leaf veins — and avoiding the tough cellulose entirely
context: Herbivorous insects host gut microbes (bacteria, fungi, protists) that digest cellulose, lignin, and detoxify plant defenses. Termites are the dramatic case — their gut protists themselves host bacteria. Endosymbiosis within endosymbiosis.

question: Hamilton's 1964 rule rb > c predicts when altruistic behavior should evolve, where r is genetic relatedness, b is benefit to recipient, c is cost to altruist. The rule predicts which feature about Hymenopteran sister relationships?
answer: Haplodiploid sex makes sister r about 0.75, above the 0.5 to daughters, so helping siblings beats raising daughters
choices: Haplodiploid sex makes sister r about 0.75, above the 0.5 to daughters, so helping siblings beats raising daughters
Inbreeding in honeybee colonies raises sister relatedness to roughly 1.0, making workers near-clones of the queen
All hive workers are genetically identical to their sisters because each hive descends from a single founding queen
Cost of reproduction is irrelevant for haplodiploids since males come from unfertilized eggs with no resource input
context: Hamilton (1964) noted Hymenopteran haplodiploidy raises full-sister r to ~0.75 (males contribute identical chromosomes). Workers raising sisters share more genes with each sister than with daughters (r=0.5). Sterile-caste evolution requires more than haplodiploidy alone.

question: The peppered moth case combines a documented population-level change with a clearly identified selection pressure. Critics in the 1990s questioned the canonical bird-predation story. What did follow-up studies by Cook, Grant, and Saccheri establish?
answer: Bird-predation survives scrutiny — predation experiments confirmed selection on resting moths and allele frequencies tracked pollution
choices: Bird-predation survives scrutiny — predation experiments confirmed selection on resting moths and allele frequencies tracked pollution
Bird-predation is wrong — moth populations shifted due to direct toxic effects of soot on dark-form metabolism each generation
The case was a forgery — original 1950s photographs were staged with dead moths pinned to bark, undermining the whole account
The case remains open — no follow-up has been able to confirm or deny what drove population shifts during the 19th century
context: Sargent et al. (1998), Cook (2003), Grant (2007), Saccheri et al. (2008) — Majerus's predation experiments and identification of the cortex locus confirmed selection on bird-visible resting moths plus a known mutation source. Hooper's contrarian 2002 book is widely refuted.

question: Most ant species fight intensely between colonies of the same species. Argentine ants outside their native range form continent-spanning supercolonies that cooperate. What does this loss of intercolonial aggression most plausibly reflect?
answer: Genetic bottleneck — invasive populations descend from few founders, reducing recognition-cue diversity below the discrimination threshold
choices: Genetic bottleneck — invasive populations descend from few founders, reducing recognition-cue diversity below the discrimination threshold
Group selection — cooperating supercolonies outcompete fighting colonies, so cooperation evolved adaptively in the invasive range
Pheromone evolution — Argentine ants in the new range gained novel chemicals that suppress the aggression triggers in workers
Cultural learning — ants pass down cooperation through behavioral imitation between worker generations on the new continents
context: Tsutsui, Suarez, Holway, Case (PNAS, 2000): Linepithema humile in California has dramatically reduced genetic diversity in cuticular hydrocarbon recognition cues compared to native Argentine populations. With fewer foreign signatures to recognize, neighbors test as nestmates.

question: In 1860 Darwin wrote to Asa Gray: 'I cannot persuade myself that a beneficent and omnipotent God would have designedly created the Ichneumonidae with the express intention of their feeding within the living bodies of caterpillars.' What was Darwin describing?
answer: Parasitoid wasps lay eggs inside caterpillars — the larvae eat the host alive, saving vital organs last to keep the meal fresh
choices: Parasitoid wasps lay eggs inside caterpillars — the larvae eat the host alive, saving vital organs last to keep the meal fresh
Wasps that infest beehives and steal honey while killing worker bees — a brutal but rapid predation Victorian naturalists noticed
A single rare wasp from Madagascar — its biology had just been described in detail at a recent British Association meeting
Caterpillars that eat their own siblings while still inside the egg case — used by Darwin in early notes on natural selection
context: Ichneumonid (and braconid) parasitoid wasps lay eggs inside or on living caterpillars. Larvae consume non-vital tissue first, keeping the host alive as long as possible. Darwin's 1860 letter to Asa Gray frames it as a serious problem for natural-theology design arguments.

question: California's Central Valley grows ~80% of the world's almonds. Each February, the orchards bloom — but California's resident pollinators cannot meet the demand. What policy and logistical system makes the crop possible?
answer: Trucked honeybees — beekeepers move colonies from across the US, with the almond crop alone requiring roughly 70% of all commercial US hives
choices: Trucked honeybees — beekeepers move colonies from across the US, with the almond crop alone requiring roughly 70% of all commercial US hives
Wild-bee subsidies — federal payments compensate California for protecting native bee habitat near each almond grove and orchard
Hand pollination — laborers brush pollen onto each blossom by hand during a tight three-week February pollination window
Closed greenhouses — almonds are now grown indoors with managed insect populations to avoid weather risk in February
context: Commercial honeybee migration: California almonds require ~2 million hives in February. The trucking event is the largest planned pollination service in human history. Colony Collapse Disorder threatens this system; varroa mite control and habitat are policy concerns.

question: Honeybee colony decline since 2006 has been linked to multiple stressors at once. Which framing best represents the scientific consensus on the cause?
answer: Multiple stressors combining — varroa mites, neonicotinoid pesticides, pathogens, and habitat loss interact; no single factor alone explains the decline
choices: Multiple stressors combining — varroa mites, neonicotinoid pesticides, pathogens, and habitat loss interact; no single factor alone explains the decline
Solely neonicotinoid pesticides — a single class of insecticides is the dominant driver, and bans on them have already reversed the decline in tested regions
Solely climate change — warmer winters disrupt overwintering bee colonies, and pesticide effects have been ruled out by recent studies
Solely the varroa mite — invasive parasites alone explain the decline, with pesticides and habitat loss playing no measurable role at all
context: USDA/NIFA, EPA, and EFSA reviews converge on multifactorial cause: Varroa destructor + viruses + pesticides (neonics implicated as one factor) + nutrition + habitat. Single-cause narratives oversimplify; the policy debate over neonics is ongoing.

question: The domesticated silkworm Bombyx mori has been bred for 5,000+ years for silk production. Compared to its wild ancestor Bombyx mandarina, the domestic form shows changes that disable it in the wild. Which of these changes is real?
answer: Adults cannot fly, larvae cannot find food, the species cannot survive at all without ongoing care from human keepers
choices: Adults cannot fly, larvae cannot find food, the species cannot survive at all without ongoing care from human keepers
Domestic silkworms are larger versions of the wild form, otherwise identical in survival ability across many habitats
Domestic and wild forms can no longer interbreed, since they are reproductively isolated by recent completed speciation
Domestic silkworms have lost their silk glands but produce a softer thread from completely different specialized cells
context: Bombyx mori: flightless adults (reduced wings/muscles), poor predator response, cannot locate food. Total dependency on humans. Sericulture is the oldest example of complete insect domestication. Goldsmith & Marec (2010) review the genetics.

question: Beyond haplodiploidy, what other condition is now considered key to the evolution of eusociality in bees, ants, and wasps? Boomsma and others have emphasized one trait of the ancestral queens.
answer: Monogamy — the founding queen mated with one male, making all daughters fully related, satisfying Hamilton's rule for sterile castes to evolve
choices: Monogamy — the founding queen mated with one male, making all daughters fully related, satisfying Hamilton's rule for sterile castes to evolve
Cold tolerance — ancestral queens that survived freezes built up the larger colonies that selected for division of labor over time
Long life span — queens living over a decade allowed worker generations to overlap, which is required before sterile workers can evolve
Aggressive territoriality — ancestral nests defended large territories, which only specialized workers could maintain at the size needed
context: Boomsma's 'monogamy hypothesis' (2007, 2009): all known origins of eusociality in Hymenoptera occurred in lineages with strict monogamy at the founding-queen stage. Single mating makes full-sister relatedness ~0.75 — the precondition for sterile-caste evolution.

question: A male crab infected by Sacculina develops broader abdomen and altered grooming behavior typical of a female crab — and tends the parasite's brood. Dawkins called such cases 'extended phenotypes.' What does the term mean?
answer: Parasite genes express effects in the body and behavior of another organism — the host — beyond the parasite's own body
choices: Parasite genes express effects in the body and behavior of another organism — the host — beyond the parasite's own body
A phenotype that extends throughout the host's whole life cycle — even after the parasite has died within the host body
Extra physical features on the parasite — they arise from long evolutionary contact with one specific host species over time
Genes that extend beyond DNA into behavioral patterns — shaped purely by environment, not by hereditary genetic inheritance
context: Dawkins' extended phenotype (1982): genes can express phenotypic effects outside the body that carries them. Beaver dams, spider webs, and parasite-modified host behavior are extended phenotypes. Sacculina + crab is a textbook example.

question: About a third of humans worldwide carry the parasite Toxoplasma gondii latently — usually with no obvious symptoms. Some studies have looked for behavioral effects in carriers. Which of the following honestly characterizes the state of the evidence?
answer: Suggestive but inconclusive — modest correlations with reaction time, risk-taking, and certain conditions exist, but human causation is hard
choices: Suggestive but inconclusive — modest correlations with reaction time, risk-taking, and certain conditions exist, but human causation is hard
Definitively confirmed — Toxoplasma has been shown to cause increased risk-taking and traffic accidents in carriers under controlled trials
Definitively refuted — no behavioral effect of Toxoplasma in humans has ever been found in any study published to date in the literature
Public health crisis established — most carriers show major personality changes, and this finding has prompted national screening efforts
context: Flegr and others report correlations (risk-taking, slower reaction, schizophrenia, traffic accidents). Sutterland et al. meta-analysis found effects but noted replication weakness. Animal-model causality is solid; human effect size is contested. Honest gloss: real signal, weaker than headlines.

question: A bacterium called Wolbachia infects roughly half of all insect species. It is passed from mothers to offspring through eggs. Wolbachia manipulates host reproduction in striking ways. Which of these is one of its real strategies?
answer: Killing male embryos — leaving only daughters, who can then transmit the bacterium to the next generation
choices: Killing male embryos — leaving only daughters, who can then transmit the bacterium to the next generation
Forcing males to grow extra wings — increasing dispersal so the bacterium spreads geographically faster across regions
Triggering longer lifespans in queens — so colonies live to produce more eggs total to spread the bacterium
Making infected insects more visible to predators — so they get eaten and release Wolbachia into the food web
context: Wolbachia's tricks include male-killing, cytoplasmic incompatibility (only matched-strain crosses produce offspring), feminization, and parthenogenesis induction — all increasing transmission through females. Werren et al. reviews. Wolbachia is now being released to fight dengue.

question: Ophiocordyceps unilateralis infects carpenter ants in tropical forests. Hughes et al. (2011) examined the precise spot where infected ants bite leaves before dying. What pattern did the researchers find?
answer: Death-grip sites cluster at specific heights and leaf orientations — humidity and temperature there are optimal for fungal spores
choices: Death-grip sites cluster at specific heights and leaf orientations — humidity and temperature there are optimal for fungal spores
Death-grip sites are random across all leaves — the fungus has no positional preference, only the timing of host death matters
Death-grip sites occur only on the underside of leaves — where the ant happens to be when fungal control of motion fails entirely
Death-grip sites correspond exactly to the worker's home nest location — never more than a meter from the nest's actual entrance
context: Hughes et al. (PLoS ONE, 2011): ant 'death grips' cluster ~25 cm above forest floor, on north-facing leaf veins. Microhabitat is fungus-optimal. The fungus drives the host to a specific microclimate before killing — among the most elegant cases of parasite manipulation.

question: Coconut crabs are the largest terrestrial arthropods alive — but populations are declining across the Pacific. Conservation efforts emphasize what core measure?
answer: Regulated harvest with size limits and breeding-season closures — combining traditional Pacific Islander harvest with documented sustainable take
choices: Regulated harvest with size limits and breeding-season closures — combining traditional Pacific Islander harvest with documented sustainable take
Total no-take preserves closing all coconut-crab islands to any human contact at all — permanent exclusion as the sole core measure used
Captive breeding programs — wild populations are now being phased out entirely and replaced by hatchery-released individual coconut crabs
Predator control — removing all native birds and invasive rats from coconut crab islands across the Pacific now as the central measure
context: Birgus latro conservation under IUCN: regulated harvest with size minimums, gravid female closures, and traditional management. Sustained-use models on Niue, Vanuatu, and elsewhere. Pure no-take preserves are less common — and reduce the income that funds enforcement.

question: Justin Schmidt's 1990s pain index rates Hymenoptera stings on a 1-4 scale based on duration and quality. The velvet ant 'cow killer' scores at the high end. Schmidt's broader project was meant to do what?
answer: Quantify defensive sting pain across species — relating each species' pain quality to the chemistry and ecology of its venom
choices: Quantify defensive sting pain across species — relating each species' pain quality to the chemistry and ecology of its venom
Develop pain medications by isolating active compounds in the strongest stings — those ranked at the top of his entire scale
Rank insects by how dangerous they are to humans medically — guiding public health decisions about insect bite and sting risk
Test his own pain tolerance against published animal averages — comparing his data with comparable medical-pain study results
context: Schmidt's Sting Pain Index (1990) ranks Hymenoptera stings 1.0-4.0 with descriptions (bullet ant: 'walking over flaming charcoal with a 3-inch nail in your heel'). His broader work links venom chemistry to ecology and evolution — not just shock value.

question: Bombardier beetle defensive chemistry is sometimes raised by anti-evolution writers as a case selection cannot explain — 'how would each step in the assembly survive?' What is the evolutionary biologist's standard reply?
answer: Each precursor step has plausible function alone — peroxide and quinones serve defense in many beetles, with intermediate chemistry in relatives
choices: Each precursor step has plausible function alone — peroxide and quinones serve defense in many beetles, with intermediate chemistry in relatives
The bombardier beetle is in fact intelligently designed — biologists privately concede this case lies outside the explanatory range of selection
The bombardier beetle evolved its full system in a single mutation event — preserved exactly as found from the moment it first appeared on Earth
The bombardier beetle's spray is not actually hot — earlier reports of 100°C were measurement errors that have now been corrected by labs
context: Isaak (TalkOrigins) and Eldredge address this: hydrogen peroxide and quinones are defensive in many arthropods. Each precursor step is plausibly functional. Related beetles (carabids) show intermediate chemistry. The irreducible-complexity framing misreads developmental history.

question: Vinegaroons, spiders, scorpions, and harvestmen are all arachnids — yet each is in its own taxonomic order. What does this tell us about how the arachnid lineage diversified?
answer: Arachnids underwent ancient adaptive radiation — by the Devonian, distinct orders had specialized for different niches
choices: Arachnids underwent ancient adaptive radiation — by the Devonian, distinct orders had specialized for different niches
All modern arachnid orders descend from spiders — other groups diverged from the spider lineage in the last 100 million years
Arachnid orders evolved through hybridization — between scorpions and spiders during the Mesozoic before continental drift
Arachnid orders are taxonomically arbitrary — convenient labels with no real evolutionary basis and no shared ancestry within
context: Arachnida diverged early on land. Devonian-Carboniferous fossils show distinct orders (Araneae, Scorpiones, Opiliones, Acari, Thelyphonida) already present. The arachnid common ancestor was likely Silurian. Each order represents a deep, separate adaptive radiation.

question: A 'daddy longlegs' is widely believed to be a spider with the world's most powerful venom. The first claim is half wrong. What is actually true about the harvestmen people call daddy longlegs?
answer: They are not true spiders — Opiliones is a separate arachnid order, and harvestmen have no venom glands or silk glands at all
choices: They are not true spiders — Opiliones is a separate arachnid order, and harvestmen have no venom glands or silk glands at all
They are spiders but with fangs too small to bite humans — their venom is real but cannot break human skin under any circumstance
They are spiders with venom too weak to harm any other animal — even small insects survive the bite easily and recover unharmed
They are insects — six legs and three body segments — only mistakenly grouped together with spiders by old naturalists in error
context: Harvestmen (Opiliones) are arachnids but NOT spiders (Araneae). They lack venom glands, lack silk glands, and have a single fused body. Cellar spiders (Pholcus) — also called daddy longlegs — ARE spiders but produce mild venom. Two animals share the name.

question: Adult atlas moths have no functional mouthparts. They live a week or two without eating and die after mating. Why has natural selection kept this 'capital breeding' strategy?
answer: Larvae store enough fat for adult reproduction — adult feeding offers little fitness gain compared to the mating effort required
choices: Larvae store enough fat for adult reproduction — adult feeding offers little fitness gain compared to the mating effort required
Atlas moths can no longer find food — past evolution closed off the food sources their ancestors once relied on entirely on land
Predation on adult moths is so high — feeding would waste days the moth needs for immediate mating during the short adult window
Mouthparts shrank as wings grew larger — there was no space left on the moth's head for functional feeding structures to fit on
context: Capital breeding: organism uses larval-accumulated reserves for adult reproduction rather than feeding as adult. Common in Saturniidae (atlas, luna, cecropia). Income vs capital breeding is a classic life-history axis. The trade-off favors reproduction over longevity here.

question: Eastern monarch overwintering populations in Mexico have declined ~80% since the 1990s. Several causes have been identified. Which combination of conservation responses reflects the current evidence on what would help most?
answer: Restore milkweed in the breeding range — protect Mexican overwintering forests and reduce broad-spectrum pesticide on migration
choices: Restore milkweed in the breeding range — protect Mexican overwintering forests and reduce broad-spectrum pesticide on migration
Restrict roadside mowing during the migration window — pesticide and habitat issues have been ruled out by the most recent work
Captive-breed monarchs and release them in fall — wild populations and habitat now lie beyond recovery for a real wild migration
Restore predators of monarch competitors — raising hawkmoth populations to make monarchs face less competition for milkweed
context: USFWS, Xerces Society, Monarch Joint Venture: breeding-range milkweed loss (Roundup-resistant crops removed milkweed from corn/soy fields), overwintering deforestation, climate, and pesticide stressors all contribute. The conservation toolkit is multifactor.

question: The bombardier beetle's defensive spray releases ~70 kJ/mol of heat from the catalase/peroxidase-driven reaction of hydroquinones with hydrogen peroxide. The reaction is rapid because of what?
answer: Enzyme catalysis — the catalase enzyme massively accelerates the otherwise slow oxidation, releasing energy in milliseconds for the spray
choices: Enzyme catalysis — the catalase enzyme massively accelerates the otherwise slow oxidation, releasing energy in milliseconds for the spray
Pure spontaneous reaction — no enzyme is needed at all; the chemicals react quickly without any catalyst in the beetle's chamber alone
External heat from sunlight on the beetle's back — solar input drives the reaction temperature past the ignition point repeatedly
Friction inside the chamber — moving parts inside the beetle's abdomen generate the heat that triggers each explosive release in turn
context: Bombardier beetle reaction chamber: catalases break peroxide into oxygen and water, peroxidases oxidize hydroquinones to quinones. Enzyme rate is the speed driver. The exothermic reaction heats the chamber to ~100°C in milliseconds. Aneshansley & Eisner (Science, 1969).

question: Cuttlefish are colorblind in the retina. Yet they match the color of a multicolored seafloor in seconds. Research has pointed at what mechanism that lets them match colors they technically can't see?
answer: Polarization vision plus skin chromatophores resolve patterns by brightness and texture — skin photoreceptors may sample light
choices: Polarization vision plus skin chromatophores resolve patterns by brightness and texture — skin photoreceptors may sample light
Color vision in cuttlefish was rediscovered in 2020 — earlier reports of colorblindness turned out to be measurement errors
Cuttlefish memorize previous seafloors — and replay matching color patterns when needed in new locations they have not seen
Cuttlefish hire fish guides — they follow species that signal background colors through their schooling behavior on seafloors
context: Mäthger & Hanlon (Science, 2010): cephalopod skin contains opsin photoreceptors. Hanlon's lab showed cuttlefish match background despite colorblind retinas. Polarization vision + skin photoreception + texture-matching produces near-perfect camouflage. Still being resolved.

question: Horseshoe crabs (which are arthropods, not crustaceans) have copper-based blue blood that clots violently in the presence of bacterial endotoxin. The biomedical industry has used this property for what purpose?
answer: Endotoxin testing of every injectable drug uses a horseshoe-crab-derived assay — though recombinant alternatives are now being adopted
choices: Endotoxin testing of every injectable drug uses a horseshoe-crab-derived assay — though recombinant alternatives are now being adopted
Manufacturing blood transfusions used at coral reef research stations — horseshoe blood substitutes for synthetic plasma in the field
Treating skin infections in burn victims — surgeons apply horseshoe blood directly to wounds as a natural antibiotic for daily care
Diagnosing genetic disease — horseshoe crab blood proteins act as universal markers for human chromosome damage in clinical assays
context: Limulus polyphemus blood contains LAL (Limulus amebocyte lysate) — used since the 1970s in endotoxin testing on all injectable pharmaceuticals. ~500,000 horseshoe crabs harvested annually, bled, and released. Recombinant factor C alternatives now in development.

question: When discussing pollinator conservation, scientists distinguish between native bees and managed honeybees. Why does that distinction matter for policy?
answer: Honeybees are an introduced managed species — too many hives can outcompete native bees, so policy favors habitat for both rather than honeybee subsidies alone
choices: Honeybees are an introduced managed species — too many hives can outcompete native bees, so policy favors habitat for both rather than honeybee subsidies alone
Honeybees and native bees are the same species — the distinction is purely about whether the colony is wild or kept in a hive at a beekeeper's farm
Native bees don't pollinate crops — so policy correctly focuses only on honeybee colony health and management, not on native bee habitat protection
Honeybees are a single global species — but every country has its own subspecies of honeybee, and each needs separate protective legal arrangements
context: Apis mellifera (the honeybee) is native to Europe/Africa/Asia, introduced to the Americas. Native bees (Bombus, Andrena, Osmia, etc) pollinate many crops better. Cane and others have shown honeybee 'subsidies' can displace native pollinators. Modern policy emphasizes both.

question: Aphids, cicadas, sharpshooters, and assassin bugs all belong to Hemiptera — the 'true bugs.' What anatomical adaptation defines this insect order?
answer: Piercing-sucking mouthparts in a tube called the rostrum — for tapping plant sap or animal blood while otherwise standing still
choices: Piercing-sucking mouthparts in a tube called the rostrum — for tapping plant sap or animal blood while otherwise standing still
Two pairs of wings exactly equal in size — distinguishing them from beetles or flies on any close anatomical inspection
Six legs and three body parts — although this feature is actually shared by all true insects in the entire group
Antennae longer than the body — the defining sensory feature that separates Hemiptera from beetles in keys
context: Hemiptera ('half-wing') unites insects with piercing-sucking rostrum mouthparts: aphids, cicadas, leafhoppers, assassin bugs, bedbugs, stink bugs. The mouthparts evolved once in the order. Different sub-orders differ in wing structure but share the feeding apparatus.

question: Bobbit worms grow up to three meters long, ambushing fish and crustaceans from buried tubes in tropical sandy seafloors. What role do they play in their ecosystems?
answer: Top ambush predators of soft-bottom communities — they pull fish biomass downward into burrows, feeding deep sediment food webs
choices: Top ambush predators of soft-bottom communities — they pull fish biomass downward into burrows, feeding deep sediment food webs
Detritivores cleaning bottom sediment — they break down decaying organic material as a primary recycling function in soft seafloors
Filter feeders capturing plankton — they engage in passive feeding without any active predation occurring at any point in life
Primary producers using chemosynthesis from sediment microbes — the worms are largely autotrophic in tropical reef-adjacent zones
context: Eunice aphroditois are predators, not detritivores. They are an ambush apex of soft-bottom benthic communities. Their feeding pulls vertebrate biomass into burrow systems, linking water column to deep sediment in tropical reef-adjacent habitats.

question: In southern California, the spread of Argentine ants is correlated with horned-lizard decline. What conservation lesson does this cascade illustrate?
answer: Displacing a competitor at one trophic level reshapes food webs unpredictably — invasive effects ripple beyond the species directly replaced
choices: Displacing a competitor at one trophic level reshapes food webs unpredictably — invasive effects ripple beyond the species directly replaced
Lizards must be captive-bred immediately whenever Argentine ants invade — without captive breeding lizard species would be lost in months
Argentine ants are beneficial as they replace less efficient native ants — lizards will adapt to a new prey base within several decades
All ant species are interchangeable for the lizard diet — the documented decline must have arisen from something else entirely instead
context: Suarez, Bolger, Case (1998): Argentine ant invasion replaces native harvester ants. Horned lizards (Phrynosoma) are obligate harvester-ant specialists. Cascade illustrates the indirect-effect rule: invasive impacts move through food webs, not just at the contact point.

question: In the green spoonworm Bonellia viridis, larvae that settle on bare substrate develop as large free-living females. Larvae that settle on or near a female develop as tiny dwarf males inside her. Which mechanism drives this?
answer: A pigment called bonellin from the female's proboscis masculinizes any larva that contacts it — environmental sex determination via maternal chemistry
choices: A pigment called bonellin from the female's proboscis masculinizes any larva that contacts it — environmental sex determination via maternal chemistry
Random chance — sex is decided when the larva hatches, not at settlement, and the substrate cue is illusory and not actually determinative at all
Temperature — colder substrates produce females and warmer substrates produce males, just as occurs in many reptile species across the world
Genetic determination — Bonellia has XY sex chromosomes like mammals, and the substrate cues do not actually determine sex in any real way
context: Bonellia viridis — Baltzer (1914) classic experiment. Larvae on rock → free-living centimeter female. Larvae on or near a female → tiny dwarf male inside her, less than a millimeter. Bonellin from female proboscis is the chemical cue. A celebrated case of environmental sex determination.

question: Naturalists like Alfred Russel Wallace, H.W. Bates, and Charles Darwin spent years collecting insects in the tropics. This Victorian tradition of insect collecting contributed to which scientific advance?
answer: Evolution by natural selection — comparative collections of related species across geography exposed the patterns that selection produced
choices: Evolution by natural selection — comparative collections of related species across geography exposed the patterns that selection produced
Discovery of antibiotics — Victorian entomologists isolated penicillin from beetle gut bacteria during their tropical collecting expeditions
Germ theory of disease — naturalists tracked malaria back to mosquito vectors through insect collecting work alone, with no other tools
Classification of insects into orders — the major orders had been left undefined before the Victorian collection era began in earnest
context: Wallace and Bates's Amazon and Malay expeditions, Darwin's Beagle voyage — comparative geographic collections of beetles, butterflies, and bees built the empirical case for descent with modification. Mimicry (Bates 1862, Müller 1879) emerged from this tradition.

question: A grasshopper called the desert or migratory locust transforms in appearance and behavior under crowded conditions — from a solitary green individual into a gregarious yellow-and-black swarmer. What is this called?
answer: Phase polyphenism — environmental input (density, tactile cues) shifts hormones and triggers a distinct morph from the same genome
choices: Phase polyphenism — environmental input (density, tactile cues) shifts hormones and triggers a distinct morph from the same genome
Speciation in real time — the two forms are now separate species that no longer interbreed under natural conditions in the wild
Genetic drift — random fluctuations between generations explain the appearance of two distinct physical forms in the population over time
Mimicry — the swarming form mimics another insect species and gains protection from predators during the long-distance migration phase
context: Locust phase polyphenism: one genome, two phenotypes triggered by density (tactile stimuli on the hind femur). Solitary phase is green, sedentary, low-feeding. Gregarious phase is yellow-black, hyperphagic, migratory. Tawfik et al. and Simpson's lab worked out the mechanism.

question: Insects evolved flight ~400 million years ago — the only flying invertebrates and the first flying animals on Earth. Vertebrate flight evolved later (pterosaurs, birds, bats). What does this temporal pattern suggest?
answer: Flight is rare and slow as an innovation — only four animal lineages have crossed the engineering threshold to powered flight in 600 million years
choices: Flight is rare and slow as an innovation — only four animal lineages have crossed the engineering threshold to powered flight in 600 million years
Insects evolved flight by gliding from trees — exactly the same pathway later used by birds and pterosaurs once their lineages had emerged afterward
Flight requires very light skeletons — only animals weighing under a gram can evolve true powered flight, and only insects met that requirement at first
Insects taught vertebrates how to fly — early insect swarms attracted vertebrate predators that gradually learned to follow them upward into the air
context: Powered flight evolved in four lineages: insects (Devonian, ~400 mya), pterosaurs (Late Triassic), birds (Jurassic, from theropods), bats (Eocene). Four times in 600 million years of animal life. The biomechanical and physiological threshold is high.

question: The US Endangered Species Act protects vertebrate animals visibly. It also protects invertebrates — including several insect and mussel species. Which examples reflect substantive ESA invertebrate listings?
answer: Karner blue butterfly, American burying beetle, freshwater mussels — habitat protection for these species also benefits broader ecosystem services
choices: Karner blue butterfly, American burying beetle, freshwater mussels — habitat protection for these species also benefits broader ecosystem services
Honeybees and monarch butterflies — both species are federally listed and benefit from full ESA Section 7 consultation in every land-use action
Earthworms and ladybugs — broad terrestrial protection for all common garden invertebrates is treated as a foundational ESA feature for many
Only marine corals are protected — the ESA does not actually cover terrestrial insects or freshwater mussels in any substantive policy way
context: ESA-listed invertebrates: Karner blue butterfly, American burying beetle, dozens of freshwater mussel species, several cave invertebrates, valley elderberry longhorn beetle, etc. Monarchs are 'warranted but precluded' — not formally listed. Honeybees are not native; not ESA candidates.

question: Paper wasps (Polistes fuscatus) show evidence of individual face recognition — they remember and discriminate other wasps' facial patterns. Tibbetts' lab demonstrated this. Why does this matter for understanding cognition?
answer: Face recognition was thought a vertebrate-only ability — finding it in wasps suggests social cognition has independent origins under social pressure
choices: Face recognition was thought a vertebrate-only ability — finding it in wasps suggests social cognition has independent origins under social pressure
Wasps are vertebrates with simpler nervous systems — the discovery places them on the cognitive ladder above many small mammal species today
Wasps were taught face recognition only in lab experiments — they cannot perform this skill in their natural colonies out in the wild at all
Face recognition is a basic feature of all insects — and the wasp result simply confirms what entomologists had long quietly assumed for decades
context: Tibbetts (Proc B 2002, 2011): Polistes fuscatus wasps discriminate individual face patterns and learn faster on conspecific faces than altered ones. P. metricus — less variable faces, less individual recognition. Social complexity → cognition argument. Echoed in Bombus studies.

question: Hamilton's rule rb > c states altruism evolves when relatedness times benefit exceeds cost. Nowak, Tarnita, and Wilson (2010) argued kin selection is not the foundation of eusociality. What is the current state of the debate among evolutionary biologists?
answer: Kin selection remains foundational — Abbot et al. (2011, ~140 signers) replied that inclusive fitness captures the same predictions and integrates with broader theory
choices: Kin selection remains foundational — Abbot et al. (2011, ~140 signers) replied that inclusive fitness captures the same predictions and integrates with broader theory
Nowak's group won the debate — kin selection is now generally rejected by mainstream evolutionary biology in favor of multilevel selection theory alone
Hamilton's rule was already discarded in the 1980s — Nowak's paper restated a consensus position that the field had already widely held by that time
Quantum-evolutionary models — both Hamilton's rule and Nowak's framework have been replaced over the course of the last decade or so
context: Nowak, Tarnita, Wilson (Nature 2010) argued against kin-selection priority. Abbot et al. (Nature 2011) signed by ~140 evolutionary biologists replied that inclusive fitness remains the more general and predictive framework. Hamilton's rule remains central in textbooks.

question: Darwin's 1860 letter on Ichneumonidae is often quoted in evolution and theology debates. Parasitoid wasp biology — eggs in living hosts, larvae eating non-vital tissue first — is presented as a problem for natural-theology design arguments. How does substantive Western Christian thought engage this?
answer: Classical response distinguishes general design from particular mechanism — Aquinas to Plantinga locate natural suffering in a fallen creation rather than denying the biology
choices: Classical response distinguishes general design from particular mechanism — Aquinas to Plantinga locate natural suffering in a fallen creation rather than denying the biology
Western Christian response denies parasitoid wasps exist as Darwin described — modern entomology has confirmed his account was overstated, and larvae avoid causing pain
Western Christian response treats all parasitism as a recent corruption — implying parasitoid wasps did not exist before some specific event in human history changed creation
Western Christian response treats natural suffering as illusory — animal pain is not real, so the parasitism case dissolves without engaging the underlying biology
context: Aquinas, Augustine, Lewis, Plantinga distinguish natural evil from moral evil. Predation and parasitism are biological realities; a fallen creation (or natural-evil as compatible with theistic providence) is the substantive Christian framing — not denial of the biology. The theological responses are real engagements, not evasions.

question: Argentine ant supercolonies cover thousands of kilometers without intraspecific aggression. Inclusive fitness theory says nestmate altruism requires relatedness, yet supercolony workers are no more related than random conspecifics. How do biologists currently resolve this paradox?
answer: Founder effects in the invasive range reduced recognition-cue variation so workers cannot tell each other apart — a recognition-system collapse, not adaptive group selection
choices: Founder effects in the invasive range reduced recognition-cue variation so workers cannot tell each other apart — a recognition-system collapse, not adaptive group selection
Group selection in fact dominates — supercolonies are adaptive units selected at colony level, vindicating Wynne's's old arguments against selfish-gene framing
Supercolonies are not real — close observation shows the colonies actually fight at boundaries, just less obviously than typical territorial ants do in their own native ranges
Argentine ants have evolved telepathy — current chemical-signal modeling does not capture the actual recognition mechanism their society uses to mark nestmate identity
context: Tsutsui & Suarez, Helanterä, Strassmann, Queller: 'unicoloniality' in invasive Argentine ants is widely interpreted as a recognition-system collapse — bottleneck-reduced cuticular hydrocarbon diversity below the threshold for nestmate discrimination. Likely a transient state on evolutionary timescales.

question: Dawkins's 'extended phenotype' concept (1982) holds that genes can express effects beyond the body that contains them. Sacculina's manipulation of crab behavior — making male crabs adopt female grooming behavior to tend the parasite's brood — is a paradigm case. What does this reveal about the gene's-eye view of selection?
answer: Selection acts on replicators wherever those replicator effects raise fitness — the so-called host body becomes part of the parasite's extended phenotype
choices: Selection acts on replicators wherever those replicator effects raise fitness — the so-called host body becomes part of the parasite's extended phenotype
Selection acts only at the organismal level — the parasite/host system is one organism in two parts, and extended-phenotype framing is biological poetry not substance
Selection acts at the group level — Sacculina selects for crab groups that tolerate parasitism most efficiently, raising the parasite's reproduction rate at group scale
Selection cannot act on extended-phenotype traits — they are mere by-products of host biology and never directly under selection in the technical sense Dawkins meant
context: Dawkins, The Extended Phenotype (1982): the replicator's reach extends beyond cell membranes. Parasite genes shape host behavior; beaver genes shape dam architecture. The conceptual move dissolves naive 'organism = unit of selection' framing. Sacculina, Toxoplasma, and Ophiocordyceps remain canonical illustrations.

question: Maynard Smith and Szathmáry's Major Transitions in Evolution (1995) frame eusociality as a transition from individual- to colony-level selection. Boomsma's monogamy hypothesis (2007) added a precondition. How do these frameworks fit together?
answer: Strict ancestral monogamy creates high relatedness allowing sterile worker castes to evolve; then colony-level selection takes over — the two frameworks complement, not compete
choices: Strict ancestral monogamy creates high relatedness allowing sterile worker castes to evolve; then colony-level selection takes over — the two frameworks complement, not compete
Major transitions and monogamy hypotheses are competing and incompatible accounts of eusocial origins — one of the two frameworks must be wrong, with field consensus pending
Major transitions theory does not include eusociality at all — Maynard Smith and Szathmáry excluded social insects from their framework, leaving Boomsma to address it alone
Monogamy is a consequence of eusociality not a precondition — once colonies exist, queens evolve to mate once for efficiency reasons of their own without prior kinship pressure
context: Boomsma's monogamy hypothesis and major transitions theory complement: ancestral monogamy provides the relatedness scaffolding (rb > c satisfied for sister care); colony-level adaptations (caste differentiation, division of labor) become advantageous afterward. Multi-male mating evolves AFTER eusociality, not before.

question: Wolbachia bacteria infect ~50% of arthropod species and pass maternally. They manipulate host reproduction in four ways: male-killing, feminization, cytoplasmic incompatibility, parthenogenesis-induction. Why does selection drive these specific manipulations rather than others?
answer: All four bias offspring sex ratio toward more females — and only females transmit Wolbachia maternally, spreading the bacterium
choices: All four bias offspring sex ratio toward more females — and only females transmit Wolbachia maternally, spreading the bacterium
Wolbachia first arose as male-killing — the other three manipulations evolved by random mutation alone with no adaptive logic for them
Wolbachia was originally a parasitoid wasp gene — it escaped into arthropod cytoplasm, so the manipulations reflect wasp biology
Wolbachia just makes its host less viable — the four 'manipulations' are merely side effects of cellular damage, not adaptive phenotypes
context: Werren, Baldo, Clark review (Nat Rev Micro, 2008): all four Wolbachia manipulations favor female-biased transmission. Females transmit Wolbachia through eggs; males are dead-ends. Selection on the bacterium favors strategies maximizing female production. Wolbachia is now released to suppress dengue-carrying mosquitoes.

question: Ophiocordyceps unilateralis manipulates carpenter ants to climb vegetation and bite leaves before dying — the 'death grip.' How does the fungus achieve such specific behavioral control without crossing the blood-brain barrier into ant neural tissue?
answer: Fungal hyphae penetrate ant muscle and surround muscle fibers without entering the brain — peripheral fungal compounds drive movement
choices: Fungal hyphae penetrate ant muscle and surround muscle fibers without entering the brain — peripheral fungal compounds drive movement
The fungus alters ant DNA through retroviral integration into the brain genome — recombining behavior loci on a 24-hour cycle until death
The fungus produces a single neurotransmitter analog that mimics the ant's natural climbing signal — described in a 1970s paper
The fungus mechanically drains ant fluid until the body collapses in a posture that resembles death-grip — no biochemistry involved
context: Hughes, Andersen, Mangold and colleagues: fungal hyphae fill the ant body, penetrate muscle, but largely spare the brain. Control may be peripheral — direct fungal compounds on muscle drive specific behavior. The 'zombie' lacks central control by fungus; the fungus operates the body through peripheral effects.

question: Conservation policy on pollinators sometimes presents 'save the bees' as a moral imperative. Scrutinizing the slogan: which framing matches the best evidence and most coherent ethical reasoning across native and managed pollinators?
answer: Honeybees are not 'saved' like wild species — they are managed livestock; habitat for diverse native pollinators (Bombus, mason bees, others) is the substantive conservation work
choices: Honeybees are not 'saved' like wild species — they are managed livestock; habitat for diverse native pollinators (Bombus, mason bees, others) is the substantive conservation work
All bees must be protected equally — distinguishing native bees from managed honeybees is a distraction from a broader pollinator emergency that demands immediate policy action
Beekeeping is morally suspect — the use of honeybees for agricultural pollination is a form of exploitation that conservation policy should phase out over the next decade
Bee declines are exaggerated — honeybee colonies in the US have grown over the last decade, and 'save the bees' is a marketing campaign promoted by environmental advocacy groups
context: The substantive ecological framing: honeybees are introduced managed livestock — colony losses are an economic problem with policy implications, not an extinction. Native bee declines (Bombus, several ESA-listed species) are conservation concerns. Pure 'save the bees' campaigns can mask the distinction.

question: Sericulture has been a partnership between humans and Bombyx mori for over 5,000 years. Some animal-ethics framings call this exploitation since silkworms are killed in cocoons before metamorphosis. Substantive Western stewardship traditions treat this differently. What framing best fits?
answer: The partnership is a paradigm case of substantive domestication — Bombyx mori cannot survive without humans; stewardship treats it as legitimate
choices: The partnership is a paradigm case of substantive domestication — Bombyx mori cannot survive without humans; stewardship treats it as legitimate
Sericulture is morally identical to factory farming — it should be phased out because silkworms are sentient and the practice is industrial-scale suffering
Sericulture is morally irrelevant — silkworms have no moral standing at all, so neither humane nor exploitative framings apply to their treatment
Sericulture is purely traditional — moral questions never arise for a practice with thousands of years of cultural history behind it in the world
context: Western stewardship tradition (Genesis, Aquinas, Aldo Leopold) treats human-animal partnerships as legitimate when conducted with husbandry care. Bombyx mori is dependent on humans — survival requires the partnership. Singer-style impartialism rejects this; substantive Western tradition recognizes legitimate use of domesticated species with humane treatment.

question: Genomic studies place ctenophores (comb jellies) as either sister to all other animals or sister to cnidarians + bilaterians. The phylogenetic placement matters for understanding when nervous systems evolved. Which evolutionary implication follows from the sister-to-all-animals hypothesis?
answer: Either the nervous system evolved twice independently — once in ctenophores and once in cnidarians + bilaterians — or sponges and placozoans lost theirs from a nerved ancestor
choices: Either the nervous system evolved twice independently — once in ctenophores and once in cnidarians + bilaterians — or sponges and placozoans lost theirs from a nerved ancestor
Nervous systems must have evolved in a single common ancestor of all animals — ctenophores simply inherited their nervous system with no possibility of any independent origin
Nervous systems are not a real biological category — the ctenophore debate has shown that the term should be abandoned from evolutionary biology in light of new genomic data
Ctenophore neurons are exactly like sponge cells — and so the long-standing difference between nervous and non-nervous animals collapses entirely on close molecular inspection
context: Dunn et al. (2008), Ryan et al. (Science 2013), Whelan et al. (Nat Eco Evo 2017): some analyses place ctenophores sister to all other animals. Their nervous systems use different neurotransmitters. Implication: parallel evolution of nervous systems OR secondary loss in sponges + placozoans. Active phylogenomic debate.

question: Tardigrades survive radiation doses that would kill humans many times over. Researchers identified a protein in tardigrade chromatin that protects DNA against radiation damage. What does this discovery suggest about possible biotechnology applications?
answer: Hashimoto et al. (2016) identified Dsup — expressed in human HEK293 cells, Dsup binds DNA and reduces radiation-induced damage by about 40%
choices: Hashimoto et al. (2016) identified Dsup — expressed in human HEK293 cells, Dsup binds DNA and reduces radiation-induced damage by about 40%
The protein protects only tardigrade DNA — it has no effect when transferred to other organisms because chromatin structures across taxa differ too much
Tardigrade radiation tolerance comes purely from desiccation — no specific protein contributes beyond the general cellular dehydration response in anhydrobiotes
Dsup has been shown to be actively harmful in human cell lines — and the original Hashimoto study has been formally retracted by the publishing journal Nature
